events.event_narrative: Snow began in Fairbanks the morning of December 25th and continued through the morning of Sunday the 26th with a few breaks in precipitation the evening of the 25th. The NWS office in Fairbanks reported 9.3 inches of snow through the morning of December 26th. On the morning of the 26th, the snow switched over to sleet, then to freezing rain and eventually rain as the air temperature rose above freezing by Sunday evening. For the 26th the total liquid equivalent precipitation for the day was 1.93��� (this is the combination of melted snow as well as rain). This amount was the 3rd highest value in a single calendar day in recorded history for Fairbanks. This is also the highest value in a single day to occur in the wintertime. Over an inch of the precipitation fell in the form of rain or freezing rain. This resulted in significant ice accumulation on roadways. Ice also accumulated on trees and powerlines through the evening.

Blizzard conditions and high winds occurred through the Bering Strait. The weather station at the village of Wales reported over six hours with a visibility near zero along with very strong winds gusting to 70 mph.

Blizzard conditions and high winds occurred across Kotzebue Sound. The weather station at the village of Kotzebue reported close to 16 hours with a visibility near zero along with very strong winds. Wind gusts peaked from the east to 55 mph during the afternoon of December 3rd.

Blizzard conditions and high winds occurred across the Yukon Delta. The weather station at the village of Scammon Bay reported visibility near zero for five hours along with very strong winds. Wind gusts peaked from the southeast to 51 mph during the afternoon of December 3rd.

High winds and near blizzard conditions occurred across portions of the northern Seward Peninsula and the coast from Cape Krusenstern northward. The weather station at the village of Point Hope reported wind gusts to 70 mph. Snow and blowing snow lowered visibility below one quarter of a mile at times from Kivalina north to Point Hope.

Temperatures in the -30's F along the eastern Arctic coast combined with southwest winds around 15 mph resulted in bitterly cold wind chill readings.  The Deadhorse airport reported wind chill temperatures to -64 F.

Temperatures in the -30's F along the eastern Arctic coast combined with southwest winds around 15 mph resulted in bitterly cold wind chill readings. Point Thompson airport reported wind chill temperatures to -63 F.

Blizzard conditions and high winds occurred across the northern Seward Peninsula and the coast from Cape Krusenstern northward. This was the second strong weather system to impact the region the first week of December. The weather station in the village of Kivalina reported a visibility near zero along with very strong winds. Wind gusts from the southeast to 75 mph were observed at Kivalina in the early evening of December 5th but the wind sensor had not been reporting for much of the day so it is possible peak winds were higher. Point Hope reported visibility to one half a mile at times and southeast wind gusts which peaked at 64 mph on the December 5th.

Blizzard conditions and high winds occurred across lower Noatak River Valley with near blizzard conditions in the lower Kobuk Valley. The weather station in the village of Noatak reported a visibility near zero along with very strong winds. A peak wind gust from the southeast to 60 mph was observed at Noatak in the morning of December 5th. Red Dog Mine also reported near zero visibility and peak wind gusts to 47 mph on December 5th.

Blizzard conditions and high winds occurred across Kotzebue Sound. The weather station at the village of Kotzebue reported a visibility near zero along with very strong winds. Wind gusts peaked from the east to 70 mph during the morning of December 5th with frequent gusts from 60 to 70 mph during the morning hours.

Blizzard conditions and high winds occurred across the Seward Peninsula. The weather station at the village of Buckland reported visibility near zero and occasionally below one half mile at Deering. Strong winds were also observed with wind gusts peaking from the southeast to 64 mph in Deering and to 51 mph in Buckland on December 5th.

Blizzard conditions and southeast winds gusting from 55 mph to nearly 70 mph occurred across the southern Seward Peninsula. Visibility near zero was observed in Nome, Golovin, and White Mountain. Peak wind gusts reached 58 mph at Nome, 61 mph at Golovin, and 69 mph in White Mountain during the morning hours of December 5th. Businesses and schools were closed across the region due to 5 foot or greater snow drifts and poor visibility. A structure under construction in Golovin had the front paneling ripped off and was flapping in the wind (see image).

Blizzard conditions and high winds occurred from St. Lawrence Island to the Bering Strait coast. This was the second strong weather system to impact the region the first week of December. The weather stations in the villages of Savoonga, Wales, and Teller all reported a visibility near zero along with very strong winds. Widespread southeast winds gusting from 70 to 80 mph were observed. Peak wind gusts ranged from 98 mph at Tin City, 76 mph at Savoonga, 70 mph at Gambell, and 74 mph at Wales during the late afternoon and evening of December 4th. Power outages were reported at Wales along with significant snowdrifts in the communities.

Blizzard conditions and high winds occurred across the Yukon Delta. This was the second strong weather system to impact the region the first week of December. The weather station in the villages of Scammon Bay and Mountain Village reported a visibility near zero along with very strong winds, while other communities in the region reported near blizzard conditions with visibility one half mile or less at times. Wind gusts peaked during the overnight hours of December 4th from the southeast to 75 mph at Cape Romanzof, 68 mph at Scammon Bay, and 63 mph at Mountain Village.

Heavy snow, strong winds, and near blizzard conditions impacted the Lower Yukon Valley communities. Officials at the school in Russian Mission reported a storm total of 8 inches of new snow with significant drifting. In Anvik, visibility was one half mile or less at times with southeast wind gusts peaking at 50 mph on December 5th.
Heavy snow impacted several of the middle Yukon River Valley communities. The SNOTEL at Galena reported around 13 inches during the event.

events.cz_name: S. SLOPES OF ERN BROOKS RANGE
events.event_narrative: Very heavy snow fell along the Brooks Range with the highest amounts from the Dalton Highway westward. The COOP observer in Wiseman reported an incredible storm total of 41.6 inches between 4 PM Sunday December 5th and 4 AM Tuesday December 7th. Another resident in Wiseman observed approximately 37 inches that fell between Sunday evening December 5th and Noon Monday December 6th. Amounts were lighter just to the south with the Coldfoot SNOTEL reporting a storm total of 19 inches for the event.

Heavy snow impacted several of the Upper Koyukuk River Valley communities. The weather observer in Bettles reported 13.7 inches of snow between Sunday evening December 5th and Monday afternoon December 6th.

Strong southerly Chinook winds were observed through Alaska Range passes. The AKDOT Road Weather Information System observation along the Parks Highway at Antler Creek reported a peak gust of 78 mph during the early afternoon of December 6th.

events.event_narrative: Strong southerly Chinook winds were observed through Alaska Range passes. The Ft. Greely Mesonet observation Texas Condo near the Richardson Highway reported occasional gusts to 81 mph between the evening of December 5th and the morning of December 6th.

events.event_narrative: Heavy snow and strong winds in the Alaska Range resulted in near blizzard conditions. The AKDOT Trims Maintenance Camp on the Richardson Highway reported 11 inches of storm total snowfall, poor visibility in snow and blowing snow, and heavy drifting across the highway. Winds started out as southerly and shifted to northerly in the later half of the event, which impacted different portions of the highway corridor through the Alaska Range.
Storm system brought 8 inches of snow at the Bettles Airport.

A peak wind gust of 62 mph (54 kt) reported at the Tin City AWOS.

Strong easterly winds persisted over eastern Norton Sound for over 24 hours with routine over 60 mph. The strong winds caused the schools to be cancelled in Unalakleet. The winds also caused damage to sheet metal roofing of several sheds in Unalakleet and knocked over two light poles.

Kuparuk reported wind chill values as cold a -78 degrees Fahrenheit.

events.event_narrative: Trims DOT Camp reports just 12-24 inches of snow south of the camp along the Richardson Highway in a little over 24 hours. This caused the Richardson Highway to be closed for several hours.
Kotzebue reported wind gusts as high as 55mph with consistent visibility of less than one quarter mile.
Tin City reported wind gusts as high 58 mph with visibly less than one quarter miles for over three hours.
Noatak reported gusts as high as 45 mph with visibility less than one quarter mile for over three hours.
Kivalina reported gusts as high as 41 mph with visibility less than one quarter mile for over three hours.
Point Lay reported 54 mph winds with visibility of a quarter miles for several hours.
Utqiagvik reported wind gusts as high as 48 mph with visibility less than one quarter mile for four hours.
Deadhorse reported gusts as high as 60 mph with visibility less than one quarter mile. The blizzard conditions persisted for over 24 hours.
Blizzard conditions occurred at both Barter Island and Point Thomson. The strongest winds occurred on Barter Island where winds gusted as high as 60 mph.

A COOP observer east of Delta Junction reported 12 inches of snow with this event. The snow began on the evening of the 9th and tapered off the evening of the 10th. West of Delta Junction public reports ranged from 4 to 6 inches of accumulation with this event.
Snow began in Northway just before 11 PM on the 8th, and by 11 PM on the 9th 8 inches of snow had fallen. In Tok, 9.7 inches of snow was measured by the COOP observer.
Strong winds developed in Golovin the morning of the 10th. Wind gusts at high as 75 mph occurred during the event, with the peak around 9 AM.
The Deadhorse airport reported gusts to 35 mph with visibility less than one quarter mile for just over three hours.
The Barter Island AWOS reported gusts as high as 45 mph with visibility as low as a quarter mile for just over three hours.

A persistent ground blizzard occurred at Pont Lay. Pont Lay reported consistent sustained winds in excess of 35 mph with visibility as low as a quarter mile for the better part of three days. Gusts as high as 50 mph were reported during the event.

Easterly winds with gusts as high as 49 mph developed in Point Lay the morning of April 15th. Blowing snow associated with the strong winds caused the visibility to drop down to less than one quarter mile for several hours.

Strong winds developed along the Beaufort Sea coast the morning of the 15th. Nuiqsut saw gusts as high as 42 mph while Deadhorse saw gusts as high as 35 mph. The strong winds caused blowing snow to develop at both locations with several hours where the visibility below one quarter mile.

events.event_narrative: Water levels rose to bankfull in Manley Hot Springs the evening of May 6th and by the morning of May 7th major flooding was observed in the community. NWS staff on a Civil Air Patrol reconnaissance flight observed a large ice jam on the Tanana River 12 miles downriver which dammed the river and backed up water into the community. The river crested around 9 am May 8th with a preliminary estimated stage of 19.50 feet, which is 6.0 feet above flood stage. This was the highest water level observed at Manley Hot Springs since the record flood of 1956 (the 1956 flood is estimated approximately 2.5 feet higher). The ice jam held for 36 hrs, releasing on the morning of May 8th and water levels began to recede through the day. Standing water remained in low lying areas of the community through the following week. Impacts to the community included many homes and structures either flooded or surrounded by water, many roads inundated with some parts of town appearing cut off and only accessible by boat, Only 6 of freeboard under the Manley Hot Springs Slough bridge, approximately 500 feet of the Elliot Highway approaching town was inundated with several feet of water, power was shut down in the community as a precaution due to the lines being buried, cellular, phone, and internet networks are down. In addition significant areas of fuel sheen on the water surface due to overturned heating fuel tanks and other sources.

An ice jam formed at Sand Island, adjacent to McGrath, at 5pm on May 10th . Before the ice jam, waterleaves were near bankfull, and the ice jam caused the river to rise 4.5 feet in 6 hours ��� from 19.2��� at 5 PMto 23.7��� and 11PM. The ice jam held for 26 hours, releasing at 6pm on 5/11, with the water dropping rapidly. The flooding caused damage to Chinana Avenue, the main road in town as well as the road to the dump. The flood damaged the sewage lagoon and the dump. Water entered basements and crawlspaces of around 15 homes.

An ice jam formed the evening of May 9th in that Yukon River which caused flooding in the village of Circle. This flooding caused the road to the airport to the airport to become impassable. The Steese Highway was flooded  with 12 inches of water. The high water levels caused the community well to flood requiring the well to be disinfected before it could be used again. One home had water enter the bottom floor.

Water levels on the Innoko River began rising to bankfull on Friday May 20th as floodwaters from an ice jam on the Yukon River started flowing into the Innoko River upstream of Shageluk. Water levels rose overbank in Shageluk on Saturday the 21st as the surge of water moved down the Innoko River, eventually cresting on Tuesday May 24th. Water levels in Shageluk remained above flood stage through May 30th with bankfull conditions persisting into the first week of June. Residents reported water over some roads near the river, including the road to the airport which was impassable and caused the airport to only be accessible by boat. The high water also caused significant erosion of some riverbanks.

Strong winds developed on the evening of the 25th in the Fairbanks area. Winds caused a significant number of downed trees, which led to over 75 separate power outages resulting in over 23,000 customers without power. The power outage caused 911 services in Fairbanks to be disrupted for several hours. Several small fires were started due to down power lines. Two people were injured by falling trees.
Strong winds developed over eastern Norton Sound. Shaktoolik had gusts to 61 mph and Unalakleet had gusts to 60 mph.

events.cz_name: NE. SLOPES OF THE ERN AK RNG
events.event_narrative: Over 3 inches of rain caused significant rises in creeks draining the Alaska Range from the evening of July 10th. This caused minor damage to several bridges, specifically the ones over Boulder Creek, Lower Suzy Q Creek, Upper Suzy Q Creek, Falls Creek, Gunnysack Creek, and Darling Creek. The Bridge over Bear Creek received significant damage, the approach road being washed out completely. The Richardson highway was closed between MP 281 and MP 234 for over 48 hours. Flooding also damaged a fiber optic cable which resulted in communications disruptions across the Interior.

The remnants of Typhoon Merbok brought high winds to the Yukon Delta beginning the afternoon of the 16th. The strongest winds were observed at Cape Romanzof which saw gusts as high as 91 mph. Other peak wind gusts in the Yukon Delta included 67 mph at Hooper Bay, 64 mph at the Reindeer River RAWS, 56 mph at Chevak, 54 mph at Scammon Bay, 53 mph at Marshall and 53 mph at St Marys. It should be noted that several of the aforementioned sites actually stopped reporting in the middle of the event potentially resulting in values being under reported. High winds caused rooves to peel off several structures in both Hooper Bay and Chevak. The FM radio tower in Chevak collapsed due to the strong winds.

The extratropical remnants of Typhoon Merbok brought high winds to St. Lawrence Island and the Bering Strait Coast. The Tin City airstrip saw wind gusts as high as 67 mph. Elsewhere, Teller saw gusts to 64 mph, Wales saw gusts to 59 mph, Bervig Mission saw gusts to 58 mph and Savoonga saw gusts to 48 mph.

The extratropical remnants of Typhoon Merbok brought high winds to the southern Seward Peninsula Coast Beginning the evening of the 16th and continuing into the morning of the 17th. Golovin saw gusts to 63 mph. Elsewhere, White Mountain saw gusts 60 mph while the peak wind at the Nome Airport was 56 mph.

The extratropical remnants of Typhoon Merbok brought high winds to the Chukchi Sea Coast beginning on the afternoon and continuing during the day on the 17th. Red Dog Dock saw gusts as high as 67 mph. Elsewhere, Kivalina saw gusts to 46 mph and Point Hope saw gusts to 47 mph.
A measured gust of 52 kt was reported at Shaktoolik AWOS.

The extratropical remnants of Typhoon Merbok moved north through the Bering Sea from Thursday September 15th to Saturday September 17th. Strong south to southwest winds resulted in a significant storm surge that caused water levels to rise from 8 to 18 feet above the normal high tide line, with the highest water levels observed in Norton Bay from Elim to Koyuk. This resulted in major coastal flooding at some communities. Fish camps and other structures along the coast used for hunting and gathering activities were damaged or destroyed across the region.||At Elim, it is estimated that water levels peaked at 14 feet above Mean Higher High Water Saturday afternoon but remained elevated into Sunday afternoon. Major flooding and erosion occurred in parts of the village and to the east at Moses Point.||At Koyuk, it is estimated that water levels peaked at 16 feet above Mean Higher High Water Saturday afternoon but remained elevated into Sunday afternoon. Major flooding and erosion occurred in parts of the village with at least one home lifted off the foundation.||At Shaktoolik, it is estimated that water levels peaked at 12 feet above Mean Higher High Water Saturday afternoon but remained elevated into Sunday afternoon. Moderate flooding and erosion occurred in parts of the village. Storm surge and wave runup destroyed much of the berm that protects the village from flooding, erosion damaged some roads in the village, and water pushed debris onto the west end of the runway and damaged the runway lights.||At Unalakleet, water levels peaked at 10.0 feet above Mean Higher High Water at 7AM AKDT on Saturday. Moderate flooding of low lying areas and erosion from wave runup occurred in parts of the village. Storm surge and wave runup damaged most the protective beach berm, water pushed debris on the airport ramp area, and water inundated low lying areas on the lagoon side of the village.||At St. Michael, it is estimated that water levels peaked around 8 feet above Mean Higher High Water Saturday afternoon but remained elevated into Sunday morning. Minor flooding occurred in parts of the village.||At Stebbins, it is estimated that water levels peaked around 10 feet above Mean Higher High Water Saturday afternoon but remained elevated into Sunday morning. Major flooding and erosion occurred in parts of the village. Coastal flooding caused damage to the local school, where water pipes were damaged. Two houses sustained minor damage.

The extratropical remnants of Typhoon Merbok moved north through the Bering Sea from Thursday September 15th to Saturday September 17th. Strong south to southwest winds resulted in a significant storm surge that caused water levels to rise from 3 to 8 feet above the normal high tide line. This resulted in minor coastal flooding and erosion. Some fish camps and other structures along the coast used for hunting and gathering activities were damaged or destroyed across the region.||At Teller, it is estimated that water levels peaked at 6 feet above Mean Higher High Water Saturday night but remained elevated into Sunday evening. Coastal erosion and minor flooding occurred in low lying areas in the community.||At Brevig Mission, it is estimated that water levels peaked Saturday but remained elevated into Sunday evening. Coastal erosion and minor flooding occurred in low lying areas in the community.||At Wales, it is estimated that water levels peaked around 6 feet above Mean Higher High Water Saturday but remained elevated into Sunday morning. Coastal erosion and minor flooding occurred in low lying areas in the community.||At Little Diomede, it is estimated that water levels peaked around 5 feet above Mean Higher High Water Saturday morning but remained elevated into Sunday morning. Coastal erosion and minor flooding occurred in low lying areas in the community.||At Savoonga, coastal erosion and minor flooding occurred in low lying areas in the community.||At Gambell coastal erosion and minor flooding occurred in low lying areas in the community.

The extratropical remnants of Typhoon Merbok moved north through the Bering Sea from Thursday September 15th to Saturday September 17th. Strong south to southwest winds resulted in a storm surge that caused water levels to rise from 5 to 9 feet above the normal high tide line causing major coastal flooding. Fish camps and other structures along the coast used for hunting and gathering activities were damaged or destroyed across the region.||Major flooding was observed in the village Hooper Bay with water levels peaking around 9 feet above the normal high tide level early Saturday morning and remaining high into Sunday.  Flooding caused damage to the village power grid causing a long term outage. This power outage resulted in significant food loss for the village.   Three homes floated off of their foundations, one of which was a complete loss. Flooding inundated the fuel storage tank farm causing one tank to tip over and a minor fuel spill to occur. Flooding caused damage to the bridge to the town evacuation site. Flooding also caused disruption to the village drinking water supply. ||Major flooding was observed in the village of Scammon Bay, with the water levels peaking around 7.5 feet above the normal high tide line early Saturday, with water levels remaining high into Sunday. A significant portion of the village runway was flooded. The flooding caused erosion damage to the west end of the runway.  Significant damage was done to the village dock and significant erosion occurred in the village harbor. ||Major flooding occurred in the village of Chevak, with water levels peaking early Saturday morning with water levels remaining high into Sunday.  Flooding caused a third of the residents in the village to lose power. The storm caused most fishing boats in the community to sink. Several sheds and outbuildings floated away. The tower for the village FM radio station collapsed during the storm due to the combination of flooding and high winds. Flooding caused significant damage to the village store causing a significant loss of food. The village fuel storage area was breached by floodwaters causing a fuel spill. Flooding caused damage to airfield lights and other equipment at the airport.  ||Minor flooding occurred in the village of Nunam Iqua. Water levels peaked around 8 feet above the normal high tide line early Saturday morning, with water levels remaining high into Sunday. Water came up around most structures in the village; however only 2 homes had damage. ||Minor flooding occurred in the village of Emmonak, with water levels peaking early Saturday morning and remaining high into Sunday. Erosion occurred along the riverbank, with debris piling up along in the village. Several fishing boats were damaged, with some a complete loss.  ||Minor flooding also occurred in the village of Alakanuk, peaking early Saturday morning.

The extratropical remnants of Typhoon Merbok moved north through the Bering Sea from Thursday September 15th to Saturday September 17th. Strong south to southwest winds resulted in a significant storm surge that caused water levels to rise from 8 to 13 feet above the normal high tide line, with the highest water levels observed at Golovin. This resulted in major coastal flooding and the worst flooding in nearly 50 years. Fish camps and other structures along the coast used for hunting and gathering activities were damaged or destroyed across the region.||At Golovin, it is estimated that water levels peaked at 12.5 feet above Mean Higher High Water Saturday afternoon but remained elevated around Noon on Saturday. Water breached the berm which protects the community from high water and wind driven waves and storm surge also pushed in from the beach side of the village. Major flooding and erosion occurred in village with numerous structures damaged or destroyed. Several homes were lifted off their foundations and displaced, the old runway was completely inundated with over 6 feet of water, power was out in the community, and sand and other debris was washed up into the community. Also, since it was hunting season many people have lost meat and other traditionally collected foods due to flooding of freezers or the lack of power to keep freezers running.||At Nome, water levels peaked at 8.99 feet above Mean Higher High Water at 12PM AKDT on Saturday. Major flooding and erosion occurred in the community with some structures and roads along the coast damaged or destroyed. Storm surge and wave runup washed over Front Street and washed out the Nome-Council Road east of Nome Water also backed up the Snake River and flooded areas around some hangers, high water lifted a house into the Snake River and drifted into the bridge on the river.

The extratropical remnants of Typhoon Merbok moved north through the Chukchi Sea from Saturday September 17th to Sunday September 18th. Strong south to southwest winds resulted in a storm surge that caused water levels to rise from 4 to 6 feet above the normal high tide line. This resulted in coastal erosion and minor flooding of low lying areas.||At Shishmaref, it is estimated that water levels peaked at 6 feet above Mean Higher High Water Saturday evening but remained elevated into Sunday evening. Minor flooding occurred in low lying areas along the lagoon side of the village. Wave runup caused significant erosion along the road to the landfill south of of the runway.||At Kivalina, water levels peaked at 3.95 feet above Mean Higher High Water at 9AM AKDT on Sunday. Minor flooding of low lying areas and erosion from wave runup was observed.

The extratropical remnants of Typhoon Merbok moved north through the Chukchi Sea from Saturday September 17th to Sunday September 18th. Strong south to southwest winds resulted in a storm surge that caused water levels to rise from 4 to 6 feet above the normal high tide line. This resulted in coastal erosion and minor flooding of low lying areas. IN Kotzebue, water levels peaked at 4.35 feet above Mean Higher High Water at 3AM AKDT on Sunday September 18th. Kotzebue reported minor impacts from flooding including structures (unknown number) on the west side of the lagoon with water underneath them, high water impacting areas around the Lagoon Street boat ramp, and water up to the edge of the runway.

High winds developed along the Chukchi Sea Coast on the evening of October 5th and continued into the morning of the 7th. Red Dog Dock recorded gusts as high as 76 mph while Point Hope reported gusts as high as 69 mph. In the village of Kivalina, the tin roof on the NANA (Alaska Native Corporation) building was blown off. In addition strong winds in Kivalina destroyed a small hangar and caused windows in several buildings to break. In the village of Point Hope, the wind blew over a large fuel storage tank.

Strong southwesterly winds developed along the front. The strongest winds were reported at the Tin City airstrip, where gusts as high as 78 mph were observed. Savoonga reported a peak gust of 68 mph, Teller had a peak gust of 61 mph, while Wales had a peak gust of 69 mph. The strong winds caused roof damage to the School in Wales. Winds also caused a power outage in the village of Savoonga that lasted for around 6 hours.

Strong southwesterly winds developed along the front. Cape Lisburne airstrip reported a peak gust of 90 mph during the event. The village of Pont Lay saw gusts as high as 60 mph. In addition, the winds caused damage to the roof of one home.
Strong winds winds associated with the front developed in Utqiagvik the morning of the 6th and continued into the afternoon. The winds caused roof damage to at least one home.

events.cz_name: N. BROOKS RNG COLVILLE RVR W
events.event_narrative: Strong winds developed as the front moved over the western Brooks Range. The Killik River mesonet station had a gust of 74 mph while the Knife Blade Ridge mesonet station had a gust of 68 mph.

Water levels began rising early in the morning hours on the 6th. Water levels peaked in Point Lay at approximately 6 feet above the normal high tide line in the early morning hours on the 7th. The high water levels in the village of Point Lay caused salt water to enter the freshwater lagoon that is the source of the village's dinking water. The increased wave action caused damage to a dock in Point Lay.

Water levels at Utqiagvik saw a quick rise early in the morning hours on the 6th, with the water level peaking around 4 feet above the normal high tide line the afternoon of the 6th. Water levels slowly receded on the 7th.  A primary section of the community berm was breached enough to allow ocean water to inundate some small businesses and cut off access to main areas of Utqiagvik.

Water began rising early in the morning hours of the 6th. Water levels peaked in Kivalina 4.46 feet above the normal high tide line the morning of the 7th. Minor flooding flooding of low lying was observed.

Water levels began rising early on the morning of the 6th with water levels peaking early the morning of the 7th in Kotzebue approximately 4 feet above the normal high tide line. Several structures in Kotzebue were surrounded by water.
Snow began the morning of the 12th and continued into the afternoon of the 13th. A cooperative weather observer in Tok reported a storm total of 11 inches of snow during the event.
Snow began late in the evening on the 29th. By 8AM on the 30th, the cooperative observer at Robertson River picked up 13 inches of snow.
Blizzard Conditions developed at Cape Romanzof in the early morning hours on the 25th and continued through the late evening. Winds gusted as high as 66 mph during the event.

Temperatures fell into the 30s below zero in Fairbanks. for an extended period of time between the 18th and the 23rd. The high temperature on both the 20th and 21st failed to climb above -30 degrees (F) at the Fairbanks airport. The coldest official temperature at the Fairbanks airport during this period was -39 degrees; however, other stations in the area fell below -40. While the temperatures during this period were not record setting, they did result in the death of one person. A 55 year old homeless man died of exposure in west Fairbanks.
Significant snow fell along the Chukchi Sea Coast. The Kivalina City Clerk reported a foot of snow fell in just over 24 hours.
Kelly Station Snow Depth SNOTEL (KLLA2) increased 6 in 24 hours with a storm total of 7.
Kotzebue Police Department estimated 4-6 with peak of event showing visibility reduced to a quarter mile and gusting to 49 knots.
Parks Highway at Antler Creek (ACRA2) DOT observation measured a gust of 85 mph an other observations in the area measured between 70 and 85 mph.  There were no known impacts from this wind event.

events.cz_name: NE. SLOPES OF THE ERN AK RNG
events.event_narrative: The Texas Condo (TCOA2) weather station, part of the Ft. Greely mesonet, measured 71 mph at 5:20pm on the 7th.
The PAIW ASOS measured a gust of 73 MPH and sites in the area measured from 60 to 75 MPH.

High winds developed on the 14th and continued into the evening of the 17th. The Cape Lisburne AWOS reported a peak gust of 96 mph at 1:55 PM on the 16. Winds on the 15th and 16 at Cape Lisburne were frequently over 80 mph. The village of Point Lay saw gusts as high as 50 mph on the 16th.

Strong winds developed the evening of the 15th and continued into early in the day on the 17th. The National Ocean Service gauge at the Red Dog Dock reported a gust of 72 mph the evening of the 16th. The AWOS at the Point Hope airport reported a gusts as high as 59 mph.
The event brought 8 inches of snow to the city of Shishmaref. The storm also brought 4 inches of snow to Kivalina and over 6 inches of snow to Point Hope.
The storm brought a foot of snow to the village of Noatak. The Red Dog mine reported several inches of snow fell; however, blowing snow made it difficult to measure.
A Native Corp official reported  in Wainwright reported 6 inches of snow fell in the 24 hour period. Near blizzard conditions were reported at Cape Lisburne with gusts of 70 knots at times.

Red Dog Mine began to report freezing drizzle Thursday afternoon and had a peak intensity of 3 statue miles and freezing rain on Saturday.
An automated sensor near Kiana reported 10 inches of snow within 24 hours.

Point Lay began reporting freezing rain early in the morning of the 1st with a mixture of rain and freezing rain continuing into morning of the 2nd.

Strong east winds brought blizzard conditions to Point Hope. Blizzard conditions lasted from the evening of the 1st through early in the morning of the second. Blowing snow continued during the day on the second, with several periods where the visibility dropped below one quarter mile briefly. Winds at Point Hope gusted as high as 45 mph during this event.
Blizzard conditions developed at Point Lay early in the morning on the 11th and continued through much of the day on the 12th. Northeasterly winds with gusts up to 49 mph were seen with this system.
Blizzard conditions developed early in the morning of the 14th and continued through late morning. By late morning, the visibility improved, even though the winds remained strong.
The winds gradually increased during the day on the 15th, with the peak wind gust occurring in the early evening. By late evening, the winds began to die down.
A four hour period of blizzard conditions developed at Point Hope on the afternoon of the 17th as light snow fell in an area where strong winds had persisted for several days.

Strong winds and blowing snow were reported across the Seward Peninsula on the 17th. Brevig Mission reported wind gusts as high as 67 mph. The strong winds caused the visibility as to one half mile for several hours.

Ice jam flooding started late at night on May 12th and when the Riverwatch team landed in Eagle on May 13th (early afternoon) flood waters had receded leaving stranded ice well above the bank. The USGS river gage had a preliminary crest of 42 feet at 5 AM ADT on May 13th. Moderate flood impacts included damage to the seawall with the guardrail along the seawall was destroyed, stranded ice, and flooding on the road between Eagle and Eagle Village leaving the road impassable for a week due to stranded ice. Several structures in town were damaged by ice and floodwaters, including the Falcon Inn which had a high water mark of almost 2 feet into the finished basement. Preceding the ice jam, the river was at or above bank full, with Mission Road beginning to flood late afternoon of May 12th.||Prior to the Eagle event, there were multiple significant ice jams in Canada, including a 30-mile-long jam with the toe of the ice jam located approximately 30 miles upriver from Eagle on May 12th. This jam caused major flooding in Canada. Downstream of Eagle was a mix of intact ice sheets, open water, and an ice jam 8 miles downriver from the month of the Tatonduk River. Thus, conditions were ripe for ice jams to impact Eagle once the Canadian ice jam released, which occurred late at night on May 12th.

Record flooding occurred on the evening of May 13th at Circle. The Riverwatch team flew between Eagle and Circle on the afternoon of May 13th. During the day on May 13th, an observer 28 miles upriver of Circle reported the highest water he���d ever seen. The Riverwatch team observed widespread flooding (trees inundated, islands covered in ice, river well out of bank) upriver from Circle. Ice had degraded during the day in warm conditions and the Riverwatch team saw ice start to move while they were in Circle at 5 pm May 13th. Prior to landing, the Riverwatch team observed a roughly 90-mile-long run of ice behind the breakup front. For context, that is the longest run of ice that this Riverwatch team could remember ever seeing. The Riverwatch team circled above several times after takeoff and observed ice moving, and progressive disintegration of larger ice sheets (indicating weakness and that given the momentum of the river ice jams were unlikely). The flooding came on quickly; the water rose extremely fast and major flooding was first reported at around 8 pm. There was extensive damage, with flood waters estimated to be higher than the previous flood of record, 1945. The store had water up to the ceiling of the first floor. Ice moved into town and damaged homes with stranded ice throughout the community. Most structures in the town flooded and also flooded the airport apron and taxiway. The Riverwatch team flew over the next day and did not observe evidence of ice jamming but believe that the river simply slowed at the S-curves (where the Yukon becomes more braided) and compounded with historically high water levels. By the next morning, floodwaters had receded and had dropped below the airport access road by 3 pm May 14th.

The breakup front progressed towards Fort Yukon on May 14th, finally stopping (jamming) just below Fort Yukon by late afternoon/evening. Water levels rose rapidly over bank and resulted in moderate flooding of the community. The river crested the night of the 14th. Several homes/structures were inundated with water. The tribal hall was flooded with water just up to the floor level with likely damage to the floor.  The road to the east of the Tribal Hall was breached to help reduce water levels with water flowing through the breach and back towards the Yukon River. The levee held well and prevented more significant damages. A local observer reported that water levels came to within one foot of overtopping the low spots along the levee, and estimated that the water level was similar to 1981. Water started receding early in the morning of May 15th when the ice jam released. The water took several days to fully drop back within bank.

On the lower Yukon River at Russian Mission, an ice jam formed downriver from Russian Mission near Marshall on May 21st. Major flooding began May 22nd with complete submersion of the airport runway, inundating 2-3 homes, and other miscellaneous structures. Additional homes and structures were completely surrounded by flood water for four days. The ice jam released on May 24th, which resulted in a gradual drop in water levels as the large volume of impounded water from the extensive lowland flooding between Holy Cross and Russian Mission drained. An ice jam flood warning was issued on May 22nd and was canceled on May 27th. Flood advisory products were continued until June 2nd.

An ice jam formed in the Yukon River Delta on May 27th on the South Mouth of Yukon River near Alakanuk. Extensive flooding occurred with moderate flooding at Alakanuk. Low-lying roads in the community were submerged including the access road to the airport. In addition, numerous homes which are elevated on pilings in Alakanuk had water beneath them along with extensive property flooding. Water and sewer lines were reportedly impacted in Alakanuk. The ice jam released on May 28th and ice was reported to be moving out through rotten shore fast ice into the Bering Sea. A Food Watch was issued on May 23rd and upgraded to a Flood Warning on May 27th. All flood products were canceled on June 3rd.

An ice jam formed in the Yukon River Delta on May 27th on the South Mouth of Yukon River near Alakanuk. Extensive overland flooding occurred with minor flooding Emmonak. Low-lying roads were submerged, including access road to the airport. In addition, numerous homes which are elevated on pilings in Emmonak had water beneath them along with extensive property flooding. The ice jam released on May 28th and ice was reported to be moving out through rotten shore fast ice into the Bering Sea. A Flood Watch was issued on May 23rd and upgraded to a Flood Warning on May 27th. All flood products were canceled on June 3rd.

Moderate flooding occurred in Buckland due to several ice jams on the Buckland River from May 17th to 19th. An ice jam located approximately 1 mile upriver from the community resulted in significant out-of-bank flow that was eventually routed around the jam and into the community of Buckland. Several additional jams were located on nearly all subsequent bends of the Buckland River downstream of Buckland. Backwater from these jams was also adding to the inundation of the community and surrounding tundra. Approximately 80% of the community was inundated with water, with water under or surrounding most structures; most roads were inundated and residents had to travel around town in boats; the road to the airport was only passable by boat. On May 19th, the Riverwatch team was informed by a trained spotter in Buckland that the upstream jam had been released, as did the downstream jams, and water was receding quickly and the community was no longer flooding.

Brevig Mission had two distinct periods of blizzard conditions during this event, with blizzard conditions present for much of the morning, with a second shorter period in the evening. Wales reported blizzard conditions for much of the morning of the 16th. Brevig Mission reported a peak wind gust of 48 mph during the event, while the peak wind gust at Wales was 41 mph.

Minor flooding caused caused water to inundate low lying roads, around and partially under three homes, making some areas in the community on accessible by boat. Water levels started to gradually fall on the 20th and it is estimated the ice jam released on the 21st when water levels dropped back within back at the community.

events.cz_name: S. SLOPES OF ERN BROOKS RANGE
events.event_narrative: Water levels rose rapidly on the Middle Fork of the Koyukuk River on Friday June 9th and went overbank and caused minor flooding by Saturday morning June 10th. At Wiseman, residents reported approximately 3 inches of water over the lower part of the access road into Wiseman. The high water caused bank erosion and some erosion on the Wiseman Road surface. High groundwater levels also caused flooding of the crawl space in at least one home in Wiseman along Wiseman Creek.

Water levels on the Koyukuk River at Allakaket rose overbank in low-lying areas of the community near the river on June 10th. Minor flooding was reported when the water crested early Monday morning June 12th. Water inundated the old runway by the river and overtopped Stanley Slough Road near the boat launch. A local observer reported that the high water and debris was initially coming from the Alatna River on June 10th but then coming down the Koyukuk River by June 11th. It is estimated water levels would need to rise approximately 1 additional foot to go over roads in the lower part of the village and have more significant impacts.

The main flow of the Sagavanirktok (Sag) River was diverted to the farthest west channel of the river due to aurfeis blocking the channel. The Sag River was pushed up against the Dalton Highway and began to erode the road near Milepost 403.5. On June 7th the road was closed at Milepost 403.5 due to the Sag River eroding the highway to the centerline with the threat of a total washout. This closure shut off the only road access to the oil fields on the North Slope of Alaska. The AK Department of Transportation immediately began hauling rock from a quarry 150 miles away in order to secure the road. The road reopened to one lane traffic on June 8th, although the threat of erosion continued for another week. Runoff from heavy rain and snowmelt in the headwaters of the Sag River reached Milepost 403.5 of the Dalton Highway on June 14th.

Heavy rain on snow caused Crooked Creek in Central to rise overbank and flood portions of the community. The public reported flood waters up to the doors of the Central Museum, into the parking lot of the local store, and up to 6 inches deep over the Steese Highway in Central. Residents put sandbags around the Central Museum but water still seeped in through the back door and got the carpet and floor wet. Floodwaters crested Thursday afternoon May 31st and flooding ended by Friday morning Jun 1st.

An ice jam formed in the Lower Yukon River upstream of Hill Island, on Saturday, May 18th. Water levels at Pilot Station rose slowly with water overbank and flooding roads in the lower portions of the village. As of early evening Saturday, May 18th, water surrounded the tribal office, AC store, tribal store and as many as 5 houses. At 330 pm Sunday, May 19th, trained river spotters reported the ice jam on the Yukon River downstream of Pilot Station released. Water levels were receding at Pilot Station due to the ice jam releasing by the morning of May 20th. A Flood Watch was issued on May 18th and upgraded to a Flood Warning on May 18th. The Flood Warning was cancelled on May 20th.

An ice jam formed in the Yukon River Delta near Emmonak on May 23rd. Ice started moving at Emmonak at 4 am on Thursday, May 23rd, and then stopped, with ice blocked up from bank to bank. Water was rising fast at Emmonak and flooding low-lying areas, including the road to the airport. The airport was closed and the road to the airport was flooded with water too deep for cars or trucks to pass. The staff gage at the power plant reported 2 feet. No structures were reported as of 8 am Thursday, May 23rd. At 930 am on Friday, May 24th, a trained river spotter reported that an ice jam that had formed on the Yukon River near Emmonak on Thursday May 23rd remained in place and that flooding of low-lying areas in Emmonak was occurring, including the road to the airport. As of Friday morning May 24th, no structures were flooding in Emmonak. Emmonak was reported to be at the same water level as seen in the 2023 break up flood.  At 11 am on Friday May 24th, an observer in Alaknuk reported widespread minor flooding was occurring and that the water had risen 2 feet since Thursday May 23rd. The observer reported that the road to the airport had 4 inches of water over it. Water levels at Alaknuk was reported to be 10 inches below the 2023 breakup flood. Water levels were receding and water was flowing by the morning of Saturday, May 25th. A Flood Watch was issued on May 20th and upgraded to a Flood Warning on May 23rd. The Flood Warning was cancelled on May 25th.

High water on the Porcupine River reached Fort Yukon on May 24th and caused the Sucker River to back up into low-lying areas on the east side of town and has flooded some roads east of Fort Yukon. A river observer reported at 1 pm Friday May 24th flooding of sloughs, low area, and some low-lying roads east of Fort Yukon. The observer reported that water was rising rapidly and was 6 inches to 1 foot below the low section of the runway in Fort Yukon. At 12 pm on May 27th a river observer reported that water levels had receded approximately one foot since Saturday May 25th with only a few inches of water remaining over the roadway near Liquor Store Lake. Sloughs near the airport remained just above bankfull. On May 28th at 3:07 pm, a river observer reported that water levels on the main stem Yukon River were up 1 to 2 feet from Monday May 27th with the Porcupine flow still dominating.  A few inches of water remained over the roadway near Liquor Store lake. Sloughs near the airport remained just above bankfull. Water began receding on May 29th and the Flood Warning was cancelled.  A Flood Watch was issued on May 20th and upgraded to a Flood Warning on May 24th. The Flood Warning was cancelled on May 29th.

On June 7th at 1500 AKDT, a USGS hydro technician observed an ice jam downstream of Spine road. The Kupurak Roads and Pads Foreman reported that the causeway approaches to bridges were flooded and that water went over the road on Sunday June 9th and rose Sunday night with an estimated 0.5 feet of water on the road. Water levels at the KUPA2 (Kuparuk River near Deadhorse) gage hit minor flood stage of 35.5 feet on Sunday June 9th at 0500 AKDT and rose steadily until early afternoon. There was a steep rise from mid-afternoon through 1900 AKDT to a relatively flat plateau around 36.7 feet.  The Kuparuk Roads and Pads Foreman reported water was 0.7 feet deep over the road and that vehicles were being escorted across. On June 11th at 1200 AKDT the sate at KUPA2 was around 36.3 feet. Water levels remained above minor flood stage until late morning on June 12 when recession steepened, and fell below action state by the morning of June 13th.

The Kobuk River at Kobuk responded by rising into town after the first crest on August 20th. Kobuk experienced water over roadways and beneath homes and some citizens were unable to vote due to the flooding. An additional 2 inches of rain fell between August 21st and 23rd, resulting in water once again rising into town.
