events.event_narrative: DOT/Alaska 511 reported a road closure at Eagle Summit Road due to blizzard conditions at 1235 on 12/12/25.

DOT/Alaska 511 reported blizzard conditions on their webpage, with the Dalton Highway closed near Sagwon at 1104 on 12/12/25. The reported estimated 8 inches of total snow with sites to the north, east, and south reporting 70 to 100 mph winds. Cloudy skies, falling snow, strong winds, and blizzard/whiteout conditions continued for many continuous hours and ended at 0614 on 12/13/25.
DOT/Alaska 511 reported blizzard conditions along the Dalton Highway between MP 235 through MP 245 at 1805 on 12/12/25. LSR's were issued reporting visibility as low as 0 miles at times.

The USARRAY D25KX mesonet site reported numerous wind gusts from 75 to 101 mph between 1210 on 12/12/25 to 2310 on 12/12/25. The D25KX mesonet site reported sustained winds at 50 mph, gusts of 101 mph before the warning was issued with a 100 mph gust observed at 1805 on 12/12/25. The Imnaviat Creek SNOTEL reported 7 inches of snow between 0500 on 12/12/25 to 0500 12/13/25, with higher snow amounts likely towards the east where there was more upslope mountain flow. Given that there was a road closure along the Dalton Highway, 0 mile visibility at Point Thomson for nearly 48 continuous hours, heavy snow reports, and very strong wind gusts, blizzard conditions were safely assumed to have occured.
The Monument Creek and Munson Ridge SNOTEL reported a 24 hour snow depth change of 9 inches at 1300 on 12/12/25, exceeding the minimum 7 inches in 24 hours criteria.
The Bonzana Creek SNOTEL reported a 24 hour snow depth change of 7.6 inches at 1200 on 12/12/25, exceeding the minimum 7 inches in 24 hours criteria.

events.cz_name: EIELSON AIR FORCE BASE AND SALCHA
events.event_narrative: Our COOP observer, Tom Griffith, reported a 24 hour snowfall total from 0900 on 12/12/25 to 0900 12/13/25. Additionally, there was a social media report of 10 inches of snowfall on Old Valdez trail by Harding Lake between 1747 on 12/12/25 to 0900 on 12/13/25.

The McGrath SNOWTEL (MCSA2) reported a snow depth increase of 7 inches over the course of 24 hours, verifying a Winter Storm Warning that was in effect for the region. The snow depth increased from 6 inches to 13 inches throughout the course of the day December 2nd. In addition strong winds gusting to 40 mph were observed at McGrath as the snow as falling.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS AND HIGH TERRAIN SOUTH OF THE YUKON RIVER
events.event_narrative: The Alaska DOT reported consistent wind gusts of 50 mph or higher across Eagle Summit throughout the morning hours of Saturday, December 6th. This resulted in blowing snow and visibilities well below 1/4 mile. As a result the DOT closed the road at Eagle Summit until later in the day when the winds began to subside.

Blizzard conditions occurred at Point Thompson where the AWOS (PAAD) began reporting heavy snow with southwest winds gusting over 40 mph and the visibility at 1/4 mile during the early afternoon hours of December 16th. These conditions persisted for close to 30 hours before the winds began to subside. In total, white out conditions were reported for 7 hours straight and the visibility remained at or below 1/4 mile for 36 hours.

Blizzard conditions were reported at both Point Thompson (PAAD) and Barter Island (PABA) starting during the morning hours of December 19th. At both locations the visibility remained at or below 1/4 mile as northeasterly winds consistently gusted to between 40 and 50 mph for approximately 15 hours. Heavy snowfall was also reported resulting in considerable blowing snow across the region.

The Point Thompson AWOS (PAAD) reported an extended period of visibilities at or below 1/4 mile throughout the afternoon and evening of December 31st along with a max wind gusts from the west of 43 mph. Meanwhile just to the east the Barter Island AWOS (PABA) reported 1/4 mile visibility for several hours along with a max wind gust of 55 mph.

Late in the evening of December 30th, strong NE winds developed with speeds of 30 to 35 mph and gusting to around 45 mph.  The winds combined with snowfall to produce visibilities of 1/4 mile or less at the Wales AWOS (PAIW). While the wind speed did fluctuate a bit, blizzard conditions were observed into the early morning hours of December 31st.

At the Eagle Airport (PAEG) winds increased and wind chill dropped well below -60F during the early morning hours of December 24th. With wind gusts as high as 60 mph, wind chill values were as low as -75F during the morning hours of Christmas Eve.

The Wales AWOS (PAIW) reported consistent wind gusts from the south of between 35 mph and 50 mph. At the same time the visibility was reported to be at or below 1/4 mile in heavy snow and blowing snow.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS AND HIGH TERRAIN SOUTH OF THE YUKON RIVER
events.event_narrative: The Alaska DOT reported up to 8 of snow over Eagle Summit by late morning on December 24th. Troopers reported that the visibility was near zero at times with winds blowing an estimated 30 to mph at elevations above 2000 feet. As a result, the highway at Eagle Summit was closed until the evening hours when the wind speeds began to subside.

The Rocky Point SNOWTEL (RPTA2) reported a snow depth increase of 8 inches from late afternoon December 21 through mid morning December 22. During this time frame the Nome ASOS (PAOM) reported several hours of 1/4 mile visibility in heavy snow with winds gusting 30 to 35 mph. Local media outlets reported that Bering Air cancelled 26 flights in and out of Nome as of December 23.

events.cz_name: EASTERN NORTON SOUND AND NULATO HILLS
events.event_narrative: The Unalakleet AWOS (PAUN) reported steady snowfall throughout the day on December 22nd with a period of heavy snow and visibilities dropping to 1/4 mile several times during the late morning and early afternoon hours.  ENE winds gusted to above 40 mph through much of the day. While Blizzard conditions were not consistent, there were reports of blizzard conditions ongoing through much of the day due to blowing snow.

The Noatak AWOS (PAWN) reported close to two days of near continuous snowfall. During this time frame blizzard to near blizzard conditions were reported with visibility dropping to 1/4 miles with heavy snow and blowing snow.

The Selawik AWOS (PASK) reported periodic blizzard conditions with 1/4 mile visibility at various times during the afternoon hours of December 22nd and again during the late morning and early afternoon of December 23rd as heavy snowfall was occurring.

The Buckland AWOS (PABL) reported periodic blizzard conditions throughout the afternoon hours of December 22nd as heavy snowfall occurred. Winds were sustained at 30 mph with the visibility occasionally dropping to 1/4 mile.

The Kotzebue ASOS (PAOT) reported periodic blizzard conditions throughout the afternoon hours of December 23rd as heavy snowfall occurred. Winds were sustained at 30 mph with the visibility occasionally dropping to 1/4 mile.

events.cz_name: EIELSON AIR FORCE BASE AND SALCHA
events.event_narrative: A trained spotter in Harding Lake reported a 24 hour total of 8 inches new snowfall from the morning of December 24th through the morning of December 25th. The eventual storm total at Harding Lake was 12 inches. Meanwhile public reports from social media indicated storm total snowfall of 12 to 14 inches at Salcha and 8 inches at Eielson Air Force Base.
The official snowfall observation from the NWS Fairbanks office reported a 24 hour snow total of 7.6.

Multiple posts to a NWS Fairbanks Facebook request for snowfall totals on the afternoon of December 24th revealed 8 to 9 inches of new snowfall over the past 24 hours. Additional snowfall was reported by the Nenana AWOS (PANN) through the afternoon and early evening hours.

events.cz_name: NE. SLOPES OF THE ERN AK RNG
events.event_narrative: The wind frequently gusted to 60 mph with a peak wind gust of 71 mph observed at the Texas Condo U.S. Army Mesonet site at 10:15 pm on the evening of the 9th.

events.cz_name: S. SLOPES OF ERN BROOKS RANGE
events.event_narrative: The cooperative observer in Wiseman reported a storm total of 13 inches of snow.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS AND HIGH TERRAIN SOUTH OF THE YUKON RIVER
events.event_narrative: The AKDOT reported hazardous road conditions at Eagle summit from miles markers 101 to 114. Blowing and drifting snow was reported with poor visibility of below 1/4 mile at times. Southwest winds were reported to be sustained at 40 mph for several hours.

Steady snow fell throughout the day on January 16th with heavy snowfall and visibilities dropping to 1/4 mile or less during the afternoon hours. Nearby the Dahl Creek SNOTEL (DHLA2) reported a 10 inch increase in snow depth throughout the day of January 16th.

The Wales Airport AWOS (PAIW) reported multiple hours of heavy snow and visibilities at or below 1/4 mile in blowing snow. Blizzard conditions prevailed throughout the day as winds remained elevated at speeds of 35 mph or greater.

The Savoonga AWOS (PASA) reported blizzard conditions throughout the morning hours and into the afternoon as local observations revealed heavy snow and visibilities at or below 1/4 mile. Winds were routinely in the 40 to 45 mph range with a peak gust of 58 mph recorded just prior to midday.

events.cz_name: EASTERN NORTON SOUND AND NULATO HILLS
events.event_narrative: The Shaktoolik AWOS (PFSH) reported a period of blizzard conditions during the afternoon and evening hours of January 15th. Winds were consistently blowing at 35 mph or higher which resulted in considerable blowing snow and visibilities at or below 1/4 mile. Peak wind gusts were reported at 50 mph or greater several times during the event.

Strong east winds developed during the morning hours of January 15th at Allen Army Airfield. As the day wore on Wind gusts of 40 to 45 mph were common. By mid afternoon a peak wind gust of 73 mph was observed by the Big Delta ASOS (PABI). The winds finally subsided just prior to midnight.

events.cz_name: EASTERN ALASKA RANGE NORTH OF TRIMS CAMP
events.event_narrative: Strong winds developed early in the morning through Isabel Pass and continued into the late afternoon hours of January 16th. From mid morning until late afternoon wind gusts consistently reached 50 mph or higher. The Texas Condo Mesonet (TCOA2) registered a peak wind gust of 85 mph late morning and saw several additional gusts of 80 mph or greater into the afternoon hours.

The Point Thomson ASOS (PAAD) began reporting visibilities of 1/4 mile around midnight due to heavy snow and increasing winds. Winds consistently gusted to between 35 and 40  mph between the early morning hours of January 26th through the middle part of the afternoon resulting in a prolonged period of blizzard conditions.

Heavy snow and low visibilities were reported early in the day by the Point Hope (PAPO) AWOS. By early afternoon blizzard conditions had settled in with winds gusting between 40 and 50 mph and visibility dropping to or below 1/4 mile. These conditions persisted into the early evening hours before the visibility began to improve.

Snowfall combined with increasing winds throughout the day at Kivalina and surrounding areas. By early afternoon the Kivalina ASOS (PAVL) began reporting blizzard conditions with the visibility dropping to around 1/4 mile and wind gusts reaching 40 to 50 mph. These conditions persisted for several hours  with the visibility finally improving during the evening and overnight hours.

Shortly after midnight the Brevig Mission AWOS (PFKT) began reporting blizzard conditions. Wind gusted to between 45 and 55 mph. This combined with light snowfall and blowing snow to reduce the visibility to 1/4 mile or lower for several hours. While the visibility improved to between 1/2 mile and 1 mile as the day wore on, the strong winds continued to produce blowing snowfall through most of the day.

A long duration blizzard set in along the central Arctic coastline during the morning hours of the 27th. The Deadhorse ASOS (PASC) reported persistent wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph for almost two full days, resulting in blowing snow and visibility readings at or below 1/4 mile. The winds eventually subsided enough after 45 hours to allow for a gradual improvement in the visibility.

For the second consecutive day the Eastern Beaufort Sea coastline experienced blizzard conditions. The AWOS at Point Thomson (PAAD) began reporting wind gusts of 35 to 45 mph along with visibility reading of 1/4 mile or less. This trend continued for more than two full days resulting in a long duration blizzard that persisted for 55 hours before letting up.

Windy conditions redeveloped along the Northwest Arctic coast during the morning hours of the the 28th. While occasional light snow fell, there was plenty of blowable snow on the ground to produce a ground blizzard as the day wore on. The Atqasuk AWOS (PATQ) began reporting blowing snow and visibility readings of around 1/4 mile during the morning hours with gusts of 40 mph common. These conditions persisted into the evening hours before the winds subsided enough to allow for improving visibility readings.

Both the Chevak and Hooper Bay AWOS stations reported blizzard conditions ongoing for multiple hours. At the Chevak AWOS site (PAVA), blizzard conditions were first met on 1/4/26 at 14:15L reporting 1/4 mi visibility with 39 mph sustained winds. The peak observation at the AWOS site reported 1/4 mi visibility, heavy snow, freezing fog, and 39 mph sustained winds gusting to 51 mph on 1/4/26 at 19:56L.

The Gambell AWOS (PAGM) site first met high wind criteria on 1/5/26 at 04:42L reporting 49 mph sustained winds, gusting at 59 mph. The AWOS site reported a peak observation at 04:56L on 1/5/26 of sustained winds at 47 mph, gusting to 63 mph. Wind gusts were in the upper 50 mph range for over 10 hrs as of 15:00L on 1/5/26.

events.cz_name: EASTERN NORTON SOUND AND NULATO HILLS
events.event_narrative: The Unalakleet AWOS (PAUN) site first met high wind criteria on 1/4/26 at 19:56L reporting 48 mph sustained winds, gusting to 60 mph. The AWOS site reported a peak observation at 21:56L on 1/4/26 of 49 mph sustained winds, gusting to 64 mph.

A Vitus (Energy Company) employee reported whiteout conditions with drifting and blowing snow at 07:58L on 1/11/26. They also estimated approximately 8 inches of snow had fallen, but couldn't verify because of the on-going blowing snow conditions. A DOT report at 07:53L on 1/11/26 later estimated as much as 12 inches of snow had fallen in and around Cantwell, with heavy blowing/drifting snow and gusty winds.

The Brevig Mission AWOS (PFKT) first met blizzard criteria at 12:56L on 1/10/26 reporting 1/4 mile visibility and winds gusting to 47 mph. The AWOS site continued to report reduced visibilities between 1/4 mile to 1/2 mile, and 40+ mph winds for over 36 hours as of 12:19L on 1/11/26.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS AND HIGH TERRAIN SOUTH OF THE YUKON RIVER
events.event_narrative: An Alaska DOT report at 07:21L on 1/11/26 reported 24 hour snowfall accumulations between 6 to 10 inches on Eureka Road in Rampart. Another DOT report around 08:00L reported 16 inches of snow in Eagle Summit but was not fully verified due to blowing/drifting snow conditions.
The Bonanza Creek SNOTEL (BONA2) reported at 01:00L 7 inches of snow in 24 hours on 1/11/26.
The Nenana SNOTEL (NESA2) reported at 04:00L 7 inches of snow in 24 hours on 1/11/26.

An Alaska DOT report at 07:23L on 1/11/26 reported 12 inches of new snowfall in Manley Hot Springs between 1/10/26 to 11/11/26. Additionally, the report noted drifting snow between MP 20-25 and 28-33, making travel difficult and vehicular traffic impassable.
An Alaska DOT report at 07:17L on 1/11/26 estimated 8 inches of new snowfall in 24 hours. There were additional DOT reports that estimated 12 inches of new snowfall in Healy on 1/11/26.

Two distinct periods of blizzard conditions impacted the area. The first period began at 1500AKST on February 27 and continued through 0020AKST on February 28 at Deadhorse, with Nuiqsut observing blizzard conditions between 1545AKST and 2315AKST on the same date. The second period began at 1640AKST on February 28 and continued through 0530AKST on March 1 at Deadhorse.||During the initial wave, sustained winds of thirty-nine miles per hour with a peak wind gust of fifty-nine miles per hour and visibility less than one-quarter mile were measured by the Deadhorse ASOS (PASC) at 2053AKST on February 27. The second period of blizzard conditions developed at 1640AKST on February 28. This second wave produced sustained winds of forty miles per hour with a peak gust of fifty-six miles per hour with snow and visibility below one-quarter mile at PASC at 2253AKST on February 28.||The Blizzard Warning was downgraded to a Winter Weather Advisory at 0241AKST on February 28 then upgraded to a Blizzard Warning at 1705AKST on the same date.

Two periods of blizzard conditions impacted Point Thomson. The first period began at 0955AKST on February 27 and continued through 0055AKST on February 28. The second period started at 1435AKST on February 28 and continued through 0955AKST on March 1. ||During the initial wave, the Point Thomson Airstrip AWOS (PAAD) reported visibilities less than one-quarter mile beginning at 0815AKST on February 27. Blizzard conditions began at 0955AKST, with the verifying observation occurring at 1255AKST on February 27. During the second wave, blizzard conditions were measured at PAAD beginning at 1434 on February 28, with the verifying observation occurring at 1735AKST while conditions continued to worsen.

Blizzard conditions impacted the Western Arctic Coast. The Point Lay LRRS Airport AWOS (PPIZ) reported visibility of one-quarter mile or less in heavy snow and freezing fog beginning at 0800AKST on February 21, 2026. The third hour of continuous blizzard conditions was met at 1100AKST. During the peak of the event, PPIZ measured sustained winds of thirty-eight miles per hour with a peak gust of forty-eight miles per hour. While the Point Hope ASOS (PAPO) lacked a functional visibility sensor to verify blizzard criteria, the station frequently recorded wind gusts exceeding fifty miles per hour. Additionally, the Cape Lisburne LRRS Airport (PALU) recorded a peak wind gust of eighty-seven miles per hour during the height of the storm. Observations at Point Lay indicated blizzard conditions through 1625AKST on February 21, followed by a brief improvement until 1735AKST. Visibilities fell below one-quarter mile again at 1741AKST, with occasional gusts over thirty-five miles per hour continuing through 1830AKST. The event concluded at 1934AKST. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

A significant winter storm impacted the Northwest Arctic Coast, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1145AKST February 20 through 2101AKST February 22, 2026. While AWOS stations at Wainwright Airport (PAWI) and Atqasuk Edward Burnell Sr. Memorial Airport (PATQ) were offline during the storm, nearby reports from the  Wiley Post-Will Rogers Memorial Airport ASOS (PABR) in Utqiagvik indicated that the area likely received record or near-record precipitation. A remote observation station northeast of Wainwright (NDBCWRXA2) measured wind gusts between thirty and forty miles per hour during the period of heaviest precipitation. Based on these wind speeds and the high moisture content of the storm, it is highly probable that Wainwright and Atqasuk experienced significant blowing snow and reduced visibilities. The first verifying observation for the warning occurred at 1029AKST on February 21, when visibilities at Utqiagvik dropped to one-half mile in snow; the final verifying observation occurred at 1210AKST on February 22. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

A record-breaking winter storm impacted the Northern Arctic Coast, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1145AKST February 20 through 2101AKST February 22, 2026. The ASOS located at Wiley Post-Will Rogers Memorial Airport (PABR) in Utqiagvik measured daily record precipitation on February 21 and February 22. Total liquid equivalent precipitation for the event exceeded three tenths of an inch, surpassing the entire monthly average for February of twenty-one hundredths of an inch. The storm produced hazardous conditions including periods of visibility reduced to one-half mile in snow and significant durations with visibility below one mile. The first verifying observation for the warning occurred at 1029AKST on February 21, when visibility at Utqiagvik dropped to one-half mile. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

Blizzard conditions impacted Kivalina, where a Blizzard Warning was in effect from 0431AKST February 20 until 0843AKST February 22, 2026. The Kivalina Airport AWOS (PAVL) initially reported blizzard conditions at 2300AKST February 20, with blizzard conditions continuing through 0415AKST February 22. At 0046AKST February 21, PAVL reported one-quarter of a mile visibility in freezing fog with sustained winds of thirty-five miles per hour and a peak gust of fifty-six miles per hour. The Blizzard Warning verified at 0200AKST February 21, when PAVL reported a third hour of blizzard conditions with visibility less than one-quarter of a mile in freezing fog with sustained winds of thirty-seven miles per hour gusting to forty-eight miles per hour. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

A significant winter storm impacted the Lower Kobuk Valley, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 0431AKST on February 20 through 2059AKST on February 22, 2026. The Robert Curtis Memorial Airport AWOS (PFNO) in Noorvik first reported visibilities reduced to one-half mile in snow and freezing fog with sustained winds of twenty-nine miles per hour gusting to thirty-five miles per hour at 0739AKST on February 21. During the peak of the event, the station measured sustained winds of twenty-three miles per hour with a peak gust of thirty-five miles per hour and one-half mile visibility in snow and freezing fog. The first verifying observation for the warning occurred at 0739AKST on February 21. Hazardous conditions, including blowing snow and reduced visibilities, persisted until the warning was downgraded on February 22. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

Blizzard conditions impacted the Baldwin Peninsula, where a Blizzard Warning was in effect from 0431AKST on February 20 through 0843AKST on February 22, 2026. The Ralph Wien Memorial Airport ASOS (PAOT) in Kotzebue reported that blizzard conditions began at 0045AKST on February 21. The third hour of continuous blizzard criteria verified the warning at 0345AKST on February 21. During the peak of the event, PAOT measured visibilities of one-quarter mile in heavy snow, with sustained winds of forty-five miles per hour and a peak gust of sixty miles per hour. Blizzard conditions concluded at 1835AKST on February 21. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

Blizzard conditions impacted the Bering Strait Coast, where a blizzard warning was in effect from 0431AKST on February 20 through 0843AKST on February 22, 2026. Local Storm Reports indicated blizzard conditions occurred in Wales. The Buckland Airport AWOS (PAIW) reported visibilities of less than one-quarter mile in heavy snow and freezing fog starting at 1741AKST on February 20. At that time, the station recorded sustained winds of forty-five miles per hour with gusts to fifty-one miles per hour. The Teller Airport AWOS (PATE) reported visibilities of one-quarter mile or less in heavy snow and freezing fog beginning at 0930AKST on February 21, with blizzard conditions continuing through 2320AKST. During the peak of the event at Teller at 0940AKST on February 21, the station measured sustained winds of sixty miles per hour with a peak wind gust of sixty-seven miles per hour while reporting one-quarter mile visibility in heavy snow and freezing fog. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

A winter storm impacted the Southern Seward Peninsula Coast, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1104AKST on February 20 through 0900AKST on February 24, 2026. At 1710AKST on February 20, the Nome Airport ASOS (PAOM) reported one-quarter mile visibility in heavy snow and freezing fog with sustained winds of twenty miles per hour gusting to thirty-two miles per hour. These conditions persisted through 1900AKST on February 20, with near-blizzard conditions occurring at times thereafter. The peak of the event occurred at 1818AKST on February 20, when the station reported one-quarter mile visibility in heavy snow and freezing fog with sustained winds of twenty miles per hour and a peak gust of thirty-two miles per hour. FAA webcams and airport observations confirmed near-blizzard and whiteout conditions in Nome through the evening of February 20. The Rocky Point SNOTEL reported eight inches of snow accumulation between February 20 and February 21. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS AND HIGH TERRAIN SOUTH OF THE YUKON RIVER
events.event_narrative: A winter storm impacted the White Mountains and High Terrain South of the Yukon River, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1027AKST on February 21 through 1200AKST on February 24, 2026. The storm produced heavy snow and significant blowing and drifting snow, leading to the closure of Eagle Summit on the Steese Highway starting at 0952AKST on February 22. Local Storm Reports confirmed the hazardous travel conditions and extensive drifting. The first verifying observation for the warning occurred at 0952AKST on February 22. Conditions gradually improved over the following days, and the final verification for the event was marked when Eagle Summit was safely reopened to traffic at 1054AKST on February 25. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

A heavy snow event impacted the Upper Chena River Valley, where a winter storm warning was in effect from 1027AKST on February 21 through 1159AKST on February 24, 2026. At the Upper Chena Dome, the snow depth was measured at thirty-eight inches at 2200AKST on February 21, increasing to forty-four inches at 2200AKST on February 22, and reaching fifty inches at 2200AKST on February 23. Additionally, the Munson Ridge SNOTEL recorded a snow depth increase from forty-four inches at 0800AKST on February 23 to fifty-three inches at 0800AKST on February 24. At the peak of the event, the station recorded a snowfall rate of one inch in one hour between 0700AKST and 0800AKST on February 24. The first verifying observation for heavy snow occurred at 0800AKST on February 24. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

events.cz_name: EIELSON AIR FORCE BASE AND SALCHA
events.event_narrative: A heavy snow event impacted Eielson Air Force Base and Salcha, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1027AKST on February 21 through 1159AKST on February 24, 2026. A trained spotter reported eight and eight-tenths inches of snow accumulation between the evening of Sunday, February 22, and 2130AKST on Monday, February 23. During the event, the Eielson Air Force Base Airport (PAEI) reported visibilities as low as one-half mile in heavy snow and freezing fog. The first verifying observation for the heavy snow occurred at 2130AKST on February 23. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

A heavy snow event impacted the Goldstream Valley and Nenana Hills, where a winter storm warning was in effect from 1027AKST on February 21 through 1159AKST on February 24, 2026. The Keystone Ridge Cooperative Observer site (KERA2) recorded an increase in snow depth from thirty-three inches at 1200AKST on February 21 to thirty-five inches at 1200AKST on February 22, then reaching forty-one inches at 1200AKST on February 23. A public report northwest of Ester confirmed thirteen and one-half inches of snow accumulation. The peak of the event occurred at 1716AKST on February 22 at the Fairbanks International Airport (PAFA), where the station reported three-quarters of a mile visibility in light snow and mist. The first verifying observation for the heavy snow occurred at 1155AKST on February 24. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

A heavy snow event impacted Two Rivers, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1027AKST on February 21 through 1159AKST on February 24, 2026. A Local Storm Report indicated that eighteen inches of snow accumulation occurred five miles east of Fox. The Ladd Army Airfield ASOS, located at Fort Wainwright, reported visibilities of one-half mile in snow during the peak of the event at 1255AKST on February 23. The first verifying observation occurred at 1010AKST on February 24. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

A heavy snow event impacted Nenana, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1027AKST on February 21 through 1159AKST on February 24, 2026. The Nenana SNOTEL recorded a seven-inch increase in snow depth between 0300AKST on February 23 and 0300AKST on February 24. At 1712AKST on February 23, the Nenana Airport AWOS (PANN) reported one-quarter mile visibility in heavy snow and freezing fog. The first verifying observation for the heavy snow occurred at 0300AKST on February 24. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

A winter storm impacted the Lower Yukon River, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1121AKST on February 21 through 2112AKST on February 23, 2026. The St. Mary's Airport AWOS (PASM) reported twelve hours of one-quarter mile visibility in unknown precipitation with wind gusts between twenty and twenty-five miles per hour. Additionally, the Russian Mission Airport AWOS (PARS) reported liquid equivalent precipitation in excess of one-tenth of an inch on February 23. The first verifying observation occurred at 1450AKST on February 23, with the final verifying observation at 1833AKST on February 23. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

A heavy snow event impacted the Lower Koyukuk Valley, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1121AKST on February 21 through 2112AKST on February 23, 2026. A report from the Hozatka Lake SNOTEL confirmed eight inches of snow accumulation between 0000AKST on February 23 and 0300AKST on February 24. The first verifying observation for the heavy snow occurred at 0300AKST on February 24. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

A heavy snow event impacted the Middle Yukon Valley, where a Winter Storm Warning was in effect from 1121AKST on February 21 through 2112AKST on February 23, 2026. The Galena SNOTEL reported snow accumulation of seven inches between 0600AKST and 1800AKST on February 23. The verifying observation occurred at 1800AKST on February 23. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

events.cz_name: EASTERN ALASKA RANGE SOUTH OF TRIMS CAMP
events.event_narrative: A blizzard impacted the Eastern Alaska Range South of Trims Camp on February 25, 2026. The Department of Transportation reported whiteout conditions in Isabel Pass south of Trims Camp. Due to the dangerously low visibility and blowing snow, the Richardson Highway was closed in both directions from mile marker one hundred eighty-six to mile marker two hundred eighteen. All lanes remained closed for the duration of the event as hazardous conditions persisted. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

The Golovin AWOS site (PAGL) first reported blizzard conditions at 15:13L on 2/16 and continued to report blizzard conditions through 23:56L on 2/16. Blizzard conditions were met at 18:25L on 2/16. Winds were consistently greater than 35 mph with visibilities at or below 1/4 miles for well over 3 hours. A peak observation was recorded at 21:13L on 2/16 with sustained winds at 40 mph gusting to 55 mph, heavy snow, freezing fog, and visibility at 1/4 miles.

The Paragon Creek Snotel reported 6 inches of snow from 2/16 to 2/17. Despite this SNOTEL being on the leeward side of the mountains, given the mesoscale and synoptic set up of the event, higher snowfall totals were likely on the windward side of the mountains. Additionally, the Elim AWOS (PFEL) to the south reported consistent heavy snow and reduced visibilities between 21:45L on 2/16 through 18:30L on 2/17. This further justifies the likelihood of heavy snowfall occuring in the mountains of the central Seward Peninsula.

The Shishmaref AWOS (PASH) first reported blizzard conditions at 11:20L on 2/16 and continued through 00:15L on 2/17. Blizzard conditions were met at 14:44L on 2/16. Sustained winds were at or above 35 mph with visibilities at or below 1/4 miles for well over 3 hours. A peak observation was recorded at 22:44L on 2/16 with heavy snow, sustained winds at 44 mph gusting to 51 mph, and 1/4 mile visibility.

The Wales AWOS site (PAIW) first reported blizzard conditions at 20:10L on 2/16 and continued through 17:39L on 2/17. Blizzard conditions were met at 23:10L on 2/16. Winds were consistently greater than 35 mph with visibilities at or below 1/4 miles for well over 3 hours. A peak observation was recorded at 21:30L on 2/16 with 56 mph sustained winds gusting to 66 mph, heavy snow, ice fog, and visibility less than 1/4 miles. Wind observations went down from 21:35L on 2/16 to 02:35L on 2/17, but winds were gusting well over 50 to 60 mph on each end of the outage. Additionally, blizzard conditions stopped briefly between the hours of 04:30L to 0800L on 2/17, but quickly started again shortly afterwards.

The Hooper Bay AWOS (PAHP) first reported blizzard conditions at 12:41L on 2/16 and continued through 19:43L on 2/16. Blizzard conditions were met at 15:45L on 2/16. A nearby AWOS site at Chevak (PAVA) also reported consistent winds above 35 mph and visibilities less than or equal to 1/4 miles for over 3 hours as well. A peak observation was recorded at the Hooper Bay AWOS (PAHP) at 16:05L on 2/16 with 44 mph sustained winds gusting to 50 mph, heavy snow, ice fog, and visibility at 1/8 miles.

The Gambell AWOS (PAGM) first reported blizzard conditions at 12:29L on 2/16 and continued through 20:35L on 2/16. Blizzard conditions were met at 15:30L on 2/16. The site reported consistent winds greater than 35 mph and visibilities at or below 1/4 miles for well over 3 hours. A peak observation was recorded at 17:56L on 2/16 with 55 mph sustained winds gusting to 68 mph, heavy snow, ice fog, and visibility less than 1/4 miles.

The Kivalina AWOS (PAVL) first reported blizzard conditions at 21:40L on 2/16 and continued through 00:05L on 2/18. Blizzard conditions were met at 00:55L on 2/17. Winds were consistently above 35 mph with visibilities at or below 1/4 miles for well over 24 hours. A peak observation was recorded at 07:53L on 2/17 with sustained winds at 39 mph gusting to 62 mph, ice fog, and visibility at 1/4 miles.

The Kotzebue AWOS (PAOT) first reported blizzard conditions at 21:27L on 2/16 and continued through 02:15L on 2/18. Blizzard conditions were met at 00:30L on 2/17. Winds were consistently between 45 to 60 mph with visibilities at or below 1/4 miles for well over 24 hours. A peak observation was recorded at 00:53L on 2/17 with sustained winds at 45 mph gusting to 70 mph, blowing snow, and visibility at 1/4 miles.

The Point Lay AWOS (PPIZ) first reported blizzard conditions around 10:56L on 2/18 and continued through 15:28L on 2/19. Blizzard conditions were met at 13:56L on 2/18. Winds were consistently above 35 mph with visibilities at or below 1/4 miles throughout the event. A peak observation was recorded at 20:12L on 2/18 with sustained winds at 37 mph gusting to 43 mph, heavy snow, freezing fog, and visibility at 1/4 miles.

events.cz_name: EASTERN NORTON SOUND AND NULATO HILLS
events.event_narrative: The Elim AWOS (PFEL) reported moderate to heavy snowfall, freezing fog, and reduced visibilities down to 1/4 miles at times between 21:45L on 2/16 through 18:30L on 2/17. Numerous observations from Elim to Unalakleet reported reduced visibilities due to heavy snow the afternoon of 2/16 to 2/17. A peak observation of 1/4 miles visibility, heavy snow, and freezing fog was reported at the Elim AWOS (PFEL) at 22:36L on 2/16.

The Kelly Station SNOTEL reported a snow depth increase from 21 inches on 2/17 at 12:00L to 31 inches on 2/18 at 12:00L. The storm total snow amount for this event was 10 inches within 24 hours. This values exceeds the snowfall criteria threshold of greater than 7 inches falling in 24 hours for this forecast zone.

The Selawik AWOS (PASK) first reported winter storm conditions at 02:41L on 2/17 and continued through 21:53L on 2/17. This equates to 19 consecutive hours of heavy snow, ice fog, winds gusting at or above 30 to 35 mph, and visibilities at or below 1/2 miles. A peak observation was recorded at 16:51L on 2/17 with sustained winds at 32 mph gusting to 38 mph, heavy snow, ice fog, and visibility less than 1/4 miles.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS AND HIGH TERRAIN SOUTH OF THE YUKON RIVER
events.event_narrative: Alaska 511 first started reporting difficult road conditions along Eagle Summit MP101 to MP114 at 08:21L on 2/18. The reports detailed blowing/drifting snow conditions with icy patches, low visibilities, and winds around 30 mph. The road was closed from 14:25L on 2/19 to 09:57L on 2/20 due to blowing/drifting snow, icy patches, low visibilities, and winds around 35 mph. Conditions were at their lowest between 14:00L on 2/19 to 17:00L on 2/19 due to snow squalls in the area.

The Munson Ridge SNOTEL reported a snow depth increase from 40 inches at 16:00L on 2/18 to 50 inches at 16:00L on 2/19. The storm total snow amount for this event was 10 inches within 24 hours. This values exceeds the snowfall criteria threshold of greater than 8 inches falling in 24 hours for this forecast zone. Additionally, radar data showed frequent snow squalls over the area between the hours of 14:00L and 17:00L on 2/19. These snow squalls created winter storm conditions of blowing snow, wind gusts greater than 35 mph, visibilities at or below 1/4 miles, and whiteout conditions for multiple hours in the afternoon.

The nearby Fairbanks ASOS (PAFA) site first reported winter storm conditions at 12:20L on 2/19 and continued through 18:15L on 2/19. Radar data showed frequent snow squalls with wind gusts at or above 35 mph, visibility at or below 1/4 miles, and whiteout conditions between the hours of 14:00L on 2/19 through 17:00L on 2/19. A peak observation was recorded at 14:53L on 2/19 with light snow, blowing snow, mist, 1 miles visibility, and sustained winds at 22 mph gusting to 36 mph.

events.cz_name: EIELSON AIR FORCE BASE AND SALCHA
events.event_narrative: An Alaskan electricity company (GVEA) reported power outages during the afternoon of 2/19 due to blowing snow conditions caused by winds gusting greater than 30 mph and visibilities at or below 1/2 miles. More than 370 people were left without power for a couple of hours in the afternoon. Additionally, the Eielson AFB observation site reported a peak observation at 14:34L on 2/19 with sustained winds at 26 mph gusting to 40 mph, blowing snow, and visibility at 2.25 miles. Snow squalls occurred between the hours of 12:20L and 18:15L across the Middle Tanana Valley, further creating winter storm like conditions throughout the day on 2/19.

Just prior to midnight on the 8th, the Umiat Airfield RAWS (UMTA2) reported a wind chill value of -70 F as the air temperature dropped to -49 F and a west wind of 7 to 10 mph developed. These conditions persisted for close to 24 hours with the wind chill dropping to -70 F on several occasions.

events.cz_name: SOUTH SLOPES OF THE EASTERN BROOKS RANGE
events.event_narrative: During the morning hours of February 10th the air temperature dropped to around -50 F for several hours at Arctic Village. The Arctic Village AWOS (PARC) reported wind speeds from the North at around 5 mph which resulted in wind chill values dropping to -70 F for several hours.

Snowfall began shortly after midnight along the Yukon Delta coast and by mid morning, heavy snow and strong winds had resulted in blizzard conditions all along the coast as well as inland. The Chevak AWOS (PAVA) began reporting wind gusts in excess of 35 mph and visibilities as low as 1/4 mile shortly after 6am with full on blizzard conditions in place a few hours later. Blizzard conditions continued for approximately 16 hours with winds gusting to between 40 and 45 mph and the visibility dropping to around 1/10 mile at times.  Meanwhile along the immediate coast the Hooper Bay AWOS (PAHP) was reporting similar conditions.

Snow began falling during the early morning hours of the 10th with the heaviest snow developing a few hours later. By midday strong winds and heavy snow had become established throughout the Lower Yukon Valley. The Marshall AWOS (PADM) began reporting blizzard like conditions with wind speeds exceeding 35 mph and the visibility lowering to around 1/4 mile around midday. By mid afternoon Blizzard conditions were ongoing and the visibility fell to around 1/10 mile as winds gusted as high as 47 mph. The blizzard subsided a few hours later, but heavy snow and strong winds kept the visibility at or below one mile well into the evening hours.

Snow began along the Bering Strait Coast shortly after midnight on the 11th and picked up in intensity as the night wore on. By mid morning the visibility reported by the Brevig Mission AWOS (PFKT) had dropped to 1/4 mile with wind gusts exceeding 35 mph. Shortly after midday full on blizzard conditions were occurring with blowing snow and the visibility dropping further to near 1/10 mile. During this time frame a max wind gust of 51 mph was re corded. By late afternoon conditions began to improve a bit, but the visibility stayed well below one mile for several more hours as strong wind gusts in excess of 40 mph continued.

Snow began along the Western Arctic Coast shortly after midnight on the 11th. By mid morning on the 12th strong winds and heavy snow had brought the visibility down to around 1/4 mile at the Point Lay AWOS (PPIZ), resulting in near blizzard conditions with winds sustained around 30 mph. The visibility dropped further as winds climbed to above 35 mph shortly before midnight. Blizzard conditions continued for approximately 30 hours at Point Lay as winds gusted to between 40 and 50 mph resulting in considerable blowing snow.

Blizzard conditions returned to the Yukon Delta Coast during the late morning hours of the 13th. The Hooper Bay AWOS (PAHP) reported strong east winds gusting to between 35 and 40 miles per hour along with heavy snow and visibility readings of 1/4 mile for approximately 7 hours. The winds began to subside enough for subsequent improvements in visibility by late afternoon and the snow eventually changed over to light rain, thus ending the blizzard.

Strong northeast winds and heavy snow arrived at St Lawrence Island early on the 13th and continued throughout the day and into the wee hours of the next morning. By early afternoon the Gambell AWOS (PAGM) was reporting wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph and a visibility at or below 1/4 mile due to blowing snow. These blizzard conditions continued into the evening hours with strong winds continuing to produce near blizzard conditions well into the overnight hours before the winds finally weakened a bit.

Public reports from Stampede Road northwest of Healy indicated a snowfall total of 20.5 inches in less than 24 hours on the 14th The nearby Healy MAWS (HEAA2) indicated that the snow fell between 5 am and 10 pm with the heaviest snow likely falling during the first 8 hours of the event.
The Rocky Point Snotel (RPTA2) reported a total snowfall amount of 11 inches in 15 hours along the southern Seward Peninsula coast.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS AND HIGH TERRAIN SOUTH OF THE YUKON RIVER
events.event_narrative: As the winter storm was approaching, strong winds accompanied a front over the higher terrain northeast of Fairbanks. AKDOT personnel initially reported a closure of Eagle Summit along the Steese Highway around Noon on the 13th. The report included heavy snowfall and strong winds estimated at 40 mph or greater resulting in blowing snow and poor visibility. Heavy drifting of snow on the roadway was also reported.

A verified storm spotter on Old Murphy Dome Road reported a snow depth change of 17.7 inches between 2/17 and 2/19. This report was in direct correlation of radar observed snow squalls that occurred across the Middle Tanana Valley between the hours of 12:20L on 2/19 through 18:15L on 2/19. A peak observation was recorded at the Fairbanks ASOS site (PAFA) at 14:53L on 2/19 with sustained winds of 22 mph gusting to 36 mph, light snow, blowing snow, mist, and visibility at 1 mile.

Heavy snow developed during the morning hours of the 14th and continued for more than 20 hours before diminishing across the Fairbanks metro area and surrounding locations throughout the Middle Tanana Valley. The official snow total measured by NWS Fairbanks at the College Observatory COOP location (FAOA2) was 8.1 inches during the 24 hour period ending at 9am on the 15th. There were also numerous public reports from around the area that indicated anywhere from 8 to 12 inches of snow from this Valentines day snow storm.

The nearby Fairbanks ASOS (PAFA) site first reported winter storm conditions at 12:20L on 2/19 and continued through 18:15L on 2/19. Radar data showed frequent snow squalls with wind gusts at or above 35 mph, visibility at or below 1/4 miles, and whiteout conditions between the hours of 14:00L on 2/19 through 17:00L on 2/19. A peak observation was recorded at 14:53L on 2/19 with light snow, blowing snow, mist, 1 miles visibility, and sustained winds at 22 mph gusting to 36 mph.

The COOP observer for Minchumina (LMHA2) reported a 24 snow total of 7.4 on the morning of the 15th. There was additional snowfall that fell outside this 24 hour window resulting in a storm total snowfall of 9.5. This data was supported by observations from the Minchumina AWOS (PAMH) which showed near constant light to moderate snowfall for almost 36 hours extending from the morning of the 14th through the afternoon of the 15th.

An Alaskan electricity company (GVEA) reported power outages during the afternoon of 2/19 due to numerous snow squalls caused by winds gusting greater than 35 mph. More than 700 people were left without power for a couple of hours in the afternoon. This occurred as a direct result of radar verified frequent snow squalls occurring across the Middle Tanana Valley between the hours of 12:20L on 2/19 through 18:15L on 2/19. The nearby Fairbanks ASOS site (PAFA) reported a peak observation at 14:53L on 2/19 with sustained winds at 22 mph gusting to 36 mph, light snow, blowing snow, and visibility at 1 mile.

WFO Fairbanks employees observed from the office frequent winds gusts greater than 30 mph with visibilities at or below 1/4 miles throughout the afternoon on 2/19. These observations were further confirmed via a social media post from Alaska State Troopers reporting multiple collisions along the southbound lanes of the Richardson Highway between the 12 Mile Bridge and the second Badger Road exit due to blowing snow and low visibilities. These road closures and collisions were visible from the WFO Fairbanks office as well. Additionally, 11.5 inches of snow was recorded at the office over a two day span. A peak observation was recorded at the Fairbanks ASOS site (PAFA) at 14:53L on 2/19 with light snow, blowing snow, mist, 1 mile visibility, and sustained winds at 22 mph gusting to 36 mph.

The Nenana SNOTEL (NESA2) reported a snow depth increase of 9 inches in less than 24 hours from 2/17 at 16:00L to 2/18 at 11:00L. Additionally, an Alaska 511 report at 05:15L on 2/18 reported snowfall totals between 4 to 10 inches along the Parks Highway from MP 276 to MP 316. A peak observation was recorded at the Nenana ASOS site (PANN) at 09:21L on 2/18 with snow, ice fog, 1/4 mile visibility, and sustained winds at 14 mph gusting to 21 mph.

A trained spotter located in Healy, Alaska reported a storm total snow amount of 11 inches between the hours of 5:00L on 2/18 through 17:51L on 2/18. Additionally, a social media comment on a Facebook post reported an estimated storm total snow amount of 16.5 inches in Anderson at 19:47L on 2/18. Frequent snow squalls were observed on radar between 14:00L and 17:00L on 2/19 throughout the Middle Tanana Valley, further supporting heavy snowfall amounts across the Northern Denali Borough.

NWS Fairbanks upgraded a Winter Storm Watch to a Blizzard Warning at 1448AKST on March 5, 2026 for the northwest Seward Peninsula. The AWOS site located at Wales Airport (PAIW) first reported blizzard conditions at 1519AKST on March 6, 2026; the final verifying observation occurred at 1456AKST on March 7, 2026. At the peak of the event, PAIW recorded one-quarter mile visibility in blowing snow with winds gusting to 41 mph. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

NWS Fairbanks upgraded a Winter Storm Watch to a Blizzard Warning at 1448AKST on March 5, 2026 for the Bering Strait Coast. The AWOS site located at Brevig Mission Airport (PFKT) first reported blizzard conditions at 1215AKST on March 6, 2026; the final verifying observation occurred at 2125AKST on March 7, 2026. At the peak of the event, PFKT measured one-quarter mile visibility in blowing snow with winds gusting to 38 mph. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

NWS Fairbanks upgraded a Winter Weather Advisory to a Blizzard Warning for Kivalina and Red Dog Dock at 0751AKST on March 7, 2026. Blizzard conditions were ongoing at the time of the upgrade. The AWOS site at Kivalina Airport (PAVL) began reporting blizzard conditions at 0410AKST on March 7, 2026; the final verifying observation occurred at 2005AKST on March 7, 2026. At the peak of the event, PAVL measured zero visibility in blowing snow with winds gusting to 52 mph. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

NWS Fairbanks issued a Blizzard Warning for the Yukon Delta Coast at 0837AKST on March 7, 2026. The AWOS site at Chevak Airport (PAVA) first reported blizzard conditions at 0835AKST on March 7, 2026; the final verifying observation occurred at 1956AKST on March 7, 2026. At the peak of the event, PAVA measured zero visibility in blowing snow with winds gusting to 46 mph. The Blizzard Warning was downgraded to a Winter Weather Advisory at 2053AKST on March 7, 2026. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

NWS Fairbanks issued a Blizzard Warning for the Yukon Delta Coast at 0837AKST on March 7, 2026. The AWOS site at Chevak Airport (PAVA) first reported blizzard conditions at 0835AKST on March 7, 2026; the final verifying observation occurred at 1956AKST on March 7, 2026. At the peak of the event, PAVA measured zero visibility in blowing snow with winds gusting to 46 mph. The Blizzard Warning was downgraded to a Winter Weather Advisory at 2053AKST on March 7, 2026. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

At 1146AKST on March 7, 2026, a Winter Storm Watch was upgraded to a Blizzard Warning for the Eastern Beaufort Sea Coast. The AWOS site at Point Thomson Airstrip (PAAD) first reported blizzard conditions at 0155AKST on March 8, 2026; the final verifying observation occurred at 2055AKST on March 10, 2026. The Blizzard Warning was cancelled at 1313AKST on March 11, 2026. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

At 2048AKST on March 7, 2026, a Winter Storm Watch was upgraded to a Blizzard Warning for the Arctic Foothills. Reports from the Alaska Department of Transportation indicated initial blizzard conditions between mileposts 305 and 356 at 0723AKST on March 8, 2026. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

Winds began to increase rapidly from the west and southwest along the NE Arctic coastline during the early morning hours of March 10th. By mid morning blizzard conditions were being reported by the Point Thomson AWOS (PAAD) with wind speeds sustained at around 35 mph and gusts exceeding 40 mph. This resulted in blowing snow reducing the visibility to or below 1/4 mile for a little over 13 hours before conditions improved. A max wind gusts of 47 mph was registered shortly after midday.

For the second time in less than a week winds began to increase rapidly from the west and southwest across the Eastern Arctic coastline in response to a storm system anchored high in the Arctic. By mid morning on the 16th the Point Thomson AWOS (PAAD) was reporting blizzard conditions with sustained winds of 35 to 40 mph and gusts of 45 mph or higher. The visibility dropped to 1/4 mile or lower due to blowing snow created by these strong winds. These conditions would persist for close to 36 hours before conditions began to improve. At the storms peak, wind gusts were measured at 50 mph or greater.

The areas fourth blizzard in less than three weeks began to unfold during the late morning hours of March 20th. Winds at the Point Thomson AWOS (PAAD) topped 35 mph kicking up plenty of blowable snow and reducing the visibility to 1/4 mile. The winds would stay elevated at 35 mph with gusts to 45 mph for more than 15 hours along with visibility readings of 1/4 mile of less well into the nighttime hours. While the wind speeds remained elevated into the overnight hours, the visibility began to improve prior to dawn the next day.

Strong west and southwest winds that had been confined to the Eastern Arctic coast began to spread further west along the central Beaufort Sea coast during the late morning hours of March 20th. A little after midday, the Deadhorse ASOS (PASC) began indicating sustained winds of 30 mph with gusts to 35 mph or higher. These winds lofted snow and the blowing snow dropped the visibility to around 1/4 mile. Conditions were made worse by ice fog that also developed across the region. These blizzard conditions persisted about 8 hours before the blowing snow and winds subsided enough to allow for improvements in the visibility.

NWS Fairbanks upgraded a Winter Storm Watch to a Winter Storm Warning at 1020AKST on April 18, 2026 for the Yukon Delta Coast. On April 18, the AWOS site at Hooper Bay Airport (PAHP) first reported blizzard conditions at 1630AKST, which continued through 2210AKST before subsiding. The AWOS site at Chevak Airport (PAVA) began reporting blizzard conditions at 1856AKST on April 18 and continued to do so through 2342AKST. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

events.event_narrative: NWS Fairbanks upgraded a Winter Storm Watch to a Winter Storm Warning for the Eastern Alaska Range South of Trims Camp at 1113AKST on April 18. The Look Eyrie SNOTEL site measured 11 inches of snowfall between 1100AKST on April 19 and 1100AKST on April 20. Additionally, the Alaska Department of Transportation recorded 11 inches of snowfall along the Richardson Highway at the Trims DOT Camp (TRDA2). No fatalities, injures, or property damage were reported.

NWS Fairbanks issued a Blizzard warning at 0958AKST on April 20 for Kivalina and Red Dog Dock. The AWOS site located at Kivalina Airport (PAVL) reported blizzard conditions from 0915AKST through 1250AKST, with gusts up to 40 mph and visibilities limited to one-quarter of a mile or less. No fatalities, injuries, or property damage were reported.

NWS Fairbanks upgraded a High Wind Watch to a High Wind Warning at 1210AKST on 04/29/26. On 4/30/26 at 2120AKST the DOT site ACRA2, located approximately 8 miles south of Delta Junction recorded gusts of 63 kts. Winds peaked at ACRA2 at 2340 AKST on 04/30/26 with sustained winds of 45 kts with gusts up to 65 kts. The last verifying observation was 10 minutes later at 2350AKST on 04/30/26. No property damage, injuries, or fatalities were reported.

The Wales AWOS site (PAIW) reported blizzard like conditions beginning at 10:50 AKDT on 4/22 and continued through 21:25 AKDT on 4/22. Blizzard criteria was met at 13:50 AKDT with light snow, ice fog, 1/4 miles visibility, and 35 mph winds. A peak observation was reported at 18:50 AKDT on 4/22 with 38 mph winds gusting to 46 mph, heavy snow, ice fog, and less than 1/4 miles visibility. The Brevig Mission AWOS site (PFKT) also reported brief blizzard like conditions from 18:05 AKDT to 20:10 AKDT, but winds did not meet blizzard criteria.

The Golovin AWOS site (PAGL) first reported blizzard like conditions at 13:00 AKDT on 4/22 and continued through 19:05 AKDT on 4/22. Blizzard conditions were met at 16:10 AKDT on 4/22 with heavy snow, ice fog, 1/4 miles visibility, and 31 mph winds gusting to 37 mph. A peak observation was reported at 15:56 AKDT on 4/22 with heavy snow, ice fog, less than 1/4 miles visibility, and 32 mph winds gusting to 41 mph.

The Hooper Bay AWOS site (PAHP) reported blizzard like conditions beginning at 00:25 AKDT on 4/22 and continued through 08:50 AKDT on 4/22. Blizzard conditions were met at 03:25 AKDT on 4/22 with heavy snow, ice fog, 1/4 miles visibility, and 38 mph winds gusting to 44 mph. A peak observation was reported at 04:38 AKDT on 4/22 with heavy snow, ice fog, 1/4 miles visibility, and 43 mph winds gusting to 48 mph.

The Point Lay AWOS site (PPIZ) reported blizzard like conditions at 05:35 AKDT on 4/23 and continued through 13:05 AKDT on 4/23. Blizzard criteria was met at 08:35 AKDT on 4/23. A peak observation was reported at 06:00 AKDT on 4/23 with snow, freezing fog, less than 1/4 miles visibility, and 33 mph winds gusting to 40 mph.

events.cz_name: EASTERN ALASKA RANGE NORTH OF TRIMS CAMP
events.event_narrative: The Donnelly Dome USARRAY mesonet site (K24KX) reported a wind gust of 73 mph at 00:10 AKDT on 4/23. These strong wind gusts continued for 15 minutes until 00:25 AKDT on 4/23.

events.cz_name: EASTERN ALASKA RANGE NORTH OF TRIMS CAMP
events.event_narrative: The Alaska DOT reported 6 to 12 inches if new snowfall along the Richardson Highway just south of Donnelly Dome. They also reported considerable blowing snow as strong north winds developed through the pass.

The NWS spotter in Tok reported a storm total snowfall amount of 8.8 inches of snow. In addition reports from the Alaska DOT indicated difficult road conditions from Dot Lake to Delta Junction along the Alaska Highway due to deep snow and icy conditions along the roadway.
A total of 6 inches of snow was observed at Noatak between 8 am on the 26th and 8 am on the 27th.  An additional 3.5 inches of snow was observed between 8 am on the 27th and 8 am on the 28th.

A 979 mb low 350 miles south of Saint Lawrence Island combined with a 1033 mb ridge across Eastern Russia to produce a period of very strong wind on Saint Lawrence Island. A peak wind gust of 53 kts(61 mph) was reported at the Gambell AWOS on Saint Lawrence Island.
The cooperative observer in Galena observed 7 inches of snow with a water content of 32 hundredths of an inch from 1800AKST on the 3rd through 1800AKST on the 4th.

A 980 mb low 350 miles south of Saint Lawrence Island on the afternoon of the 4th weakened to 1002 mb near Kodiak Island on the afternoon of the 6th.  A moist flow of air from the Bering Sea brought a prolonged period of snowfall to the Bettles area.  A total of 6.7 inches of snow was observed from 7 pm on the 4th through 2 pm on the 6th.

A strong surface trough extended from a 980 mb low near the Bering Strait along the Arctic Coast and produced blizzard conditions for about 10 hours in Deadhorse.  An east wind of 35 to 45 mph with occasional gusts to 55 mph were observed. The visibility was one quarter mile or less in blowing snow from 5 pm on the 9th through 3 am on the 10th.

Ahead of a strong occluded front a period of very strong wind was observed at Wales along the Bering Strait coast.  Sustained winds of 50 to 60 mph were observed with frequent gusts to 70 mph and a peak wind gust of 68 kts (78 mph).
A strong occluded front brought a period of blizzard conditions to Kotzebue. The wind frequently gusted to 45 mph and the visibility was reduced to one quarter mile or less in snow and blowing snow.

A strong pressure gradient between a 1056 mb high across interior Alaska and a 998 low in the Chukchi Sea produced strong winds along the Western Arctic Coast. Wind gusts to 74 mph were observed at the Cape Lisburne AWOS and 61 mph at Point Lay AWOS.

events.event_narrative: The SNOTEL at Atigun Pass on the Dalton Highway reported an increase of snow on the ground of 7 inches in 18 hrs. It is estimated that higher amounts of snow fell east of the highway. Strong north winds gusting to 38 mph at Atigun Pass and 28 mph at Anaktuvuk Pass along with low visibility in blowing snow accompanied the snowfall.
The Kotzebue ASOS reported one quarter mile or less at times with a peak wind gust of 39 mph (34 kt).

In the village of Allakaket, several roads were inundated including First and Second Avenue. Water also flowed over the road adjacent to the store. Several outbuildings were flooded and/or moved to higher ground. The local observer estimates water levels would need to rise 2 feet to flood the lowest elevation house. There were no known permanent structures impacted.

Strong east winds with frequent gusts over 40 mph resulted in blizzard conditions with visibility less than 1/4 of a mile at times. The lowest conditions were reported at the village of Nuiqsut (PAQT).

Strong east winds gusting as high as 58 mph combined with falling snow resulted in blizzard conditions with visibility below 1/4 of a mile at times. The strongest winds and lowest visibility were reported at the Pt. Thompson (PAAD) oil field.

The heaviest snow fell at higher elevations across the Fortymile Country. The SNOTEL site at Jack Wade Junction on the Taylor Hwy at an elevation of 3585 feet reported a 24 hour snowfall of 8.4 inches. The COOP observer in Chicken reported 6.5 inches. Less snow was observed at lower elevations because precipitation began as rain before transitioning to snow.

The heaviest snow was reported at higher elevations in the hills north and east of Fairbanks. A resident at Milepost 46 of the Steese Hwy northeast of Fairbanks reported an estimated 24 hour snowfall of 8.0 inches. Less snow was observed at lower elevations because precipitation began as rain before transitioning to snow. In the Fairbanks area, 2 to 4 inches of snow was observed.

The heaviest snow fell at higher elevations across the Tanana Yukon Uplands. The SNOTEL site at Eagle Summit on the Steese Hwy at an elevation of 3650 feet reported an estimated total of 11 inches.  Less snow was observed at lower elevations because precipitation began as rain before transitioning to snow.

The tight pressure gradient across the Bering Strait and northern Bering Sea resulted in southerly wind gusts from 40 to over 60 mph over the marine area and along coastal capes. The strongest winds were reported at Wales (PAIW) where gusts to 61 mph were observed.
Blizzard conditions were reported at the Point Hope AWOS. The AWOS reported one quarter mile or less at times with a peak wind gust of 52 mph (45 kt).
Water and ice pushed inland along the Yukon river near Kotlik. The village of Kotlik experienced the most significant impacts. Reports of water rising and minor flooding in the village of Kotlik.

Snowfall totals from 8 to 12 inches were observed across the area with the heaviest snow near Delta Junction. The Granite Creek SNOTEL reported a storm total of 12 inches. A Storm Spotter reported a storm total of 8.3 inches near Banner Creek on the Richardson Hwy. This is about 9 miles southeast of Birch Lake. Social media reports also indicated up to 10 inches of snowfall in Salcha. The heavy snow impacted the Richardson and Alaska Highways with travel delays.
Upslope flow and abundant moisture produced an estimated 10 inches of snow at the NPS Salmon Creek RAWS.

Up to 10 inches of rain fell in Denali National Park the first 8 days of Aug 2019. Saturated soils in steep terrain resulted in multiple mudslides that impacted the Denali Park Road. A larger slide on Aug 4th closed the road at MP48 for several hours. Due to the excessive rainfall and rock/mudslides, the NPS took preventative measures and closed the road beyond MP30 Teklanika Rest Area until conditions improved.||Saturated soils combined with over 4 inches of rain the first week of August in Healy caused Dry Creek to rise overbank on Aug 6-7th and resulted in flooding.  The flooding washed out several roads, driveways, and the approach to the Tipple Bridge which is used to access infrastructure at the Usibelli Coal Mine.

events.event_narrative: A weather front dropping south from the Arctic resulted in significant upslope snowfall along the north side of the Brooks Range from the Dalton Hwy eastward.  The Imnaviat Creek NRCS SNOTEL at approximately 3000 feet in the foothills of the Brooks Range recorded an estimated 6 inches of snowfall on Aug 20-21st. The nearby UAF Toolik Field Research Station also reported accumulating snow during this event. It is likely higher amounts fell but were unreported.

Storm surge ranged from 6 to 10 feet above the normal high tide line in eastern Norton Sound. The high surge combined with southwest winds 30 to 45 mph resulted in high surf and significant wave runup. In Shaktoolik, water surrounded the village, much of the normally dry tundra was inundated, but erosion of the evacuation route out of town was the biggest impact. In Unalakleet, water was up to the AC store, the Fish processing plant, around the village and the airport was surrounded by water. In Stebbins, minor flooding was observed and a few homes were surrounded by water. Lastly, in St. Michael minor flooding of the old shipyard and erosion were the biggest impacts.

Storm surge ranged from 6 to 8 feet above the normal high tide line along the southern Seward Peninsula coast. The high surge combined with southwest winds 30 to 45 mph resulted in high surf and significant wave runup. In Nome, water inundated low lying areas near the coast and high surf caused minor erosion along the Nome-Council road. In Golovin, water completely flooded the old runway, the barge landing and there was significant erosion. The community constructed a temporary berm which helped to hold water back from entering town. Many smaller creeks were overbank due to heavy rain. Some fishnets and a boat were lost.

Storm surge ranged from 4 to 8 feet above the normal high tide line in southern Norton Sound and the Yukon River Delta. The high surge combined with southwest winds 30 to 40 mph resulted in high surf and significant wave runup. In Kotlik, Flooding reached some homes and structures and water got into the floor insulation in homes in low lying areas. There was also damage to some boardwalks and some residents lost fishing gear and other personal items. The warnings helped people to prepare and move property, such as snow machines, four wheelers, and fish nets, to higher ground or indoors.

Storm surge ranged from 3 to 5 feet above the normal high tide line in Kotzebue Sound. The high surge combined with west winds 30 to 45 mph resulted in high surf and significant wave runup. Minor flooding was reported in low lying areas in Kotzebue and around the lagoon. Water was up to the teacher housing.

Storm surge ranged from 3 to 5 feet above the normal high tide line along the Chukchi Sea coast. The high surge combined with southwest to west winds 30 to 45 mph resulted in high surf and significant wave runup. The storm caused major erosion to the sanitation road that leads to Shishmaref���s landfill. A lot of earth, rock, rip rap, cement blocks, and boulders were dislodged from the shoreline and the road structure. In addition, some subsistence fish racks were damaged by the wind and waves.

The Alaska DOT estimated that a three day storm peaked with around 4 inches of rain in 24 hours ending on Aug 3rd in the vicinity of the Jim River between Dalton Highway Mileposts 142 to 145.  Water overtopped the Highway at two locations between Jim River #3 and Douglas Cr. Water was estimated to be around 2 feet deep across the highway. The road was impassable to some vehicles. The flowing water also caused damage to the Highway.

Heavy snow ranging from 6 inches to nearly 9 inches fell across the upper Tanana Valley north to the upper Yukon River Valley. The COOP observer in Tok reported a storm total snowfall of 8.8 inches, while the COOP observer in Eagle observed 7.5 inches during the event. For Eagle, this is the highest snow depth and highest 2-day snowfall this early in the season on record. It falls short of the highest 2-day snowfall on record for September, which is 13.5 inches in late Sept 1920. Observations at Eagle go back to 1900, but with long gaps prior to the 1970s.
